Mr. Speaker, when we left off debate on Friday, we were dealing with Motion No. 31 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), my colleague, who proposed:
That Bill C-155 be amended in Clause 10 by adding immediately after line 20 at page 6 the following:
"(c) a person who in his opinion represents labour in the handling and
transportation of grain".
That particular amendment is very important because, as has been previously pointed out by Hon. Members, a history of conflict has arisen in transportation of grain. Too often I think the conflict generated has been that of a superficial nature involving many people trying to pit, as it were, labour against the farmer, or agriculture against the people who are moving the trains and unloading the grain.
[DOT] (UI5)
Of course, there are many railway unions within my own riding. These unions include those involved in running trains, seeing that the cars get moved and maintenance. There are also those who are involved in bridging and building. It would be very desirable for these many unions to have representatives at meetings of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. As has been suggested, it is certainly possible that different unions could be represented at different times.
The suggestion of my colleague for Regina West to have labour represented on such a committee is valuable because whenever there is a good management and labour working relationship, the job is accomplished much better. It is possible for those people who are working at the grassroots level to identify certain shortcomings and areas where changes are needed and bottlenecks can be cleared up in the movement of grain.
Our other concern is that health and safety always be considered. In this respect, I want to refer to the study

October 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
conducted by the NDP in its special task force report on occupational health and safety in the federal work place. Its report is entitled "Graveyard Shifts: Life and Death on the Job in Canada". On Thursday, January 22, 1981, Members of Parliament from my Party who were involved in this particular occupational health and safety task force were at a grain elevator at Thunder Bay. They made several observations which appear at page 40 of that report and I would like to put them on the record because I think it is important for those involved in the farming and labour sectors to be aware of the type of concerns that were analyzed.
They found that the most serious and obvious problem is grain dust. It is everywhere. Although it is more dense in some areas of the elevator than others, there is no area free of it. The Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) picked up a mask discarded by a sweeper who had been on the shift for less than an hour. The accumulation of the dust in that mask makes it next to impossible to breath through. I am sure that management sometimes may not be aware of these types of problems. The Hon. Member also observed that the risk of fire must also be great. In fact, there had been several recent explosions in other elevators along the terminal. However, none of the workers could remember when the last fire drill had been held in their elevator.
Why is there value in labour being represented on such committees? They have insight and experience from being involved in working conditions. It is important that some of their experiences be understood and relayed to any type of Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
1 also want to underline the link which exists between farmers and labour. Too often there seems to be people who want to try to split the two. Even within my own family, while my father worked on the farm he began to work on the railways on a seasonal basis. In a constituency such as mine there are many farmers who have gone on to work in the trades or maintenance of railways. If they had not gone on to work on the railways, their sons have done so. Of course, many have moved to western ports such as Vancouver of Prince Rupert. I have relatives who have worked on the farms and the railway in a riding and then gone to Prince Rupert.
Therefore, to try to drive a wedge between labour and farmers is to try to drive a wedge between families. There are many people on the Prairies who would not be fooled by that type of bogus wedge. In order to overcome those types of false wedges, I think it is important to see that the transport committees be represented by people involved in labour.
As the Hon. Member for Regina West has pointed out, we are sorry that we have come to this stage where the status of a labour representative on such a committee would only be that of an observer. I must say I was a bit disappointed when the Parliamentary Secretary referred us to Clause 11 and did not give any indication or guarantee that there would be an opportunity for the observers to speak up or have their voices heard. I underline that because, as my colleague mentioned, we in the New Democratic Party would be far happier to see a full-fledged member from labour on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, perhaps even a couple of members. However the membership might rotate, I think it would be important that we have that type of representation. Even if we increased the size of the committee from 18 members to 20 members, it would be highly desirable. 1 would urge the Government to consider afresh the offer made by my colleague earlier that he would be delighted to withdraw this amendment if we had some idea that a full-fledged member of labour would be represented.
I hope the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) takes that suggestion into consideration. He has some labour union people living in his riding. A substantial number of railway people live in Winnipeg, and I am sure they would be delighted to see his concern in this area.
For the sake of unity and peace in the transportation of grain, for basic human relations, for the sake of communication and for the sake of understanding, I think it is important that this motion be considered and agreed to by all Members. I would strongly urge the Government to consider having perhaps a couple of full-fledged labour representatives on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee and then we could have these matters dealt with in a way that is fair and that recognizes the human value of those who work with their hands to see that we have bread on our tables.
I think it is important that we recognize afresh that there is no such thing as an ordinary person in Canadian society. Everybody is extraordinary. Insights which labour people can bring to us on such a committee would be more than worthwhile. I would urge the House of Commons to look favourably on this motion but also to see that a full-fledged representative of labour is placed on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be here today to speak on this amendment. I spent the weekend and part of last week in the West.
You got more coverage than Mulroney did.

I was very impressed to hear the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) speak in Saskatoon and again in Regina and make a commitment to the western farmers that the Progressive Conservative Party will do everything in its power to make sure the western producers would not bear the brunt of the upgrading of the railways. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition was as disappointed as I was when he got back to the House today and found that last week the Progressive Conservatives could have put up 48 speakers on these issues but deigned to put up only seven to make a contribution to the best legislation that this House can get to.

This particular amendment is an attempt to get the voice of labour on this particular Committee. The Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) defends western farmers and this particular Bill. He has spent a considerable amount of time attempting to impute a feeling to the New Democratic Party that this particular Committee will not do any good. We know that the Committee has some flaws and that the Bill has some flaws. We also know that the total direction of this Bill as far as farmers are concerned is to reduce effectively the possibility of their survival.
Since we have the Bill before us and it seems that the Government is foolhardy enough to eliminate its chances in the West by passing the Bill or keeping it before the House, we must make it the best Bill possible. One way to make the committee work well is not, as the Hon. Member for Vegreville suggested, by eliminating any particular group, such as the co-operatives. We should bring in as many of them as possible. We made a motion to add labour to the regular Committee. This particular approach was turned down not only by the Liberals but by the Conservatives. We now allow labour at least to have an observer status. When one can only have the crumbs, I guess one accepts them. We need a strong labour voice. By having a labour member as an observer, at least there will be somebody there able to put forward labour's case.
In the last few years there have been a couple of grain handler strikes. Actually there have been very few. There are so many unions involved in the movement of grain that if one
Western Grain Transportation Act
of them strikes, it affects the whole operation. We need someone on the committee who can present the views of labour. It could work both ways. Having a labour representative will help to get out the story of labour a little better and to a few more people than would be the case with no representative on the Committee. Also labour will be able to understand a little better the position of farmers.
Every time there is a strike in the grain handling system, there is a great movement across the country to do something about the labour union. I am a farmer. 1 know that the movement of grain is important, but 1 think the time has come when we have to look at who pays the penalty for a strike. When there is a strike in the grain handling system, farmers are affected by the possibility that their grain will not be sold as quickly as it would have. Eventually they will be able to sell their grain, but they may have to carry it over a few weeks or months longer. If affects them because they are paying interest on money and it stops their cash flow. It also' affects the labourers, those working in every facet of the grain-moving operation. They are the ones to go without wages for the period of time the union is on strike.
In addition, a large number of elevators are involved in grain handling. They are paid for this handling of grain. Whether they handle it now or later does not make much difference as they will still be paid. When the grain is not moving, they are paid for storing it. Therefore, even while the unions are on strike the grain elevator companies including to co-ops go on collecting the storage charges. The grain handling strike does not affect the elevator companies. They are not affected the same way as the farmers, and obviously the union members who go without wages.
It is time the House looked at the penalties consequent upon a strike. There are two sides to every strike. If only labour pays the penalty, the grain companies collect storage charges as well as handling the grain later, whether this week, next week or two weeks down the road, they do not have much to lose. It is time that Parliament looked at imposing some kind of penalty on the other people involved in a strike.
Labour has made concessions to make the movement of grain more smooth over the years. If labour can be more knowledgeable about the needs of the system, I am sure we can find some kind of arrangement whereby labour will not always be on the outside. The Leader of the Opposition does not think that we should "Swedenize" industry in Canada. 1 say to him that "Swedenizing" must be pretty good because Swedish industry has fewer days lost to strikes than any other country. Labour is part of the discussion on every development in Sweden. That is what we should have here.

Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to say a few words on Motion No. 31. It is important that there be worker representation on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. The reason is that the railways will not run, the ships will not be loaded and the grain will not be sold unless the workers in the system co-operate. Since the workers

October 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
are so important to the whole industry, it is only common sense that they have representation on the Committee.
My only disappointment with the Minister and other Members is that under the motion to be moved by the Minister, the working person or labour union person on the Committee will have observer status only. 1 urge the Minister to ensure that the union person be a full voting member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. It is important that the working people have a full voice. They are as important in managing the railways as the railway companies themselves. They are a very important part of the system and must be fully represented.
As has been said in this debate, there have been many strikes in our grain-moving industry. There are several different unions, such as the grain services union, the longshoremens' union, the railway unions, the grain handlers' union and so on. We on the Prairies become very frustrated when a union goes on strike and the system breaks down. One way of having a more efficient system and averting a strike is to ensure that workers have full participation at the table and more involvement in the management of their industry. There is no one better than the worker in managing the industry because he is the one who handles the cars and works with the equipment. If that person is fully represented, the system will operate much more efficiently.
The time has come to give the ordinary worker a much greater say at the bargaining table in terms of how companies should be managed. We in this country tend to cheer Solidarity and Lech Walesa in Poland. We all applaud the tremendous fight which he and Solidarity are putting up in that country. Until they were so cruelly and autocratically put down, the one thing they were campaigning for in Poland was worker control and participation in the management of industries. In addition to the straight political democracy that we take for granted in this country, they are also campaigning for economic demcora-cy. In that regard, Solidarity in Poland was ahead of what is the reality in this country. If we are going to applaud them for what they stand for in their country, then we can set an example in this country by making sure that we practice economic democracy.
1 am disappointed when the Minister says that he is willing to accept a labour representative on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, but only as an observer. It has to be more than an observer: it has to be a participant with full voting rights that are equal to those of the farmers, the railways and the companies. If we do that we will have a much better system. In fact, we should do this as a matter of course in all of our legislation or all of our companies and Crown corporations. If we did that, we would have a much more efficient economy. Canadians would tend to pull together, work together and co-operate to make their own industry much more productive.
I will give an example. In my Province of Saskatchewan, we have SED Systems, a high-tech firm involved in the agriculture business and communications. SED Systems was responsible for building part of the Canadarm used on the American
space shuttle. This is a very successful company. The ownership of that company is interesting. There is a real mix in the democratic sense. It is owned partly by the Government of Saskatchewan, partly by the University of Saskatchewan and partly by the company workers. It is a tripartite arrangement which works very well indeed.
We should strive for that kind of arrangement in this country. With that kind of arrangement there is greater pride, interest and enthusiasm on the part of the workers to ensure that the company goes well, is productive and makes a contribution to this country.
1 will give a couple of examples of what 1 mean. On August 10 at the hearings in Regina, Mr. Hugh Wagner, the secretary-treasurer of the grain services union, appeared before the special committee. He said, and I quote:
It is also ironic that the Minister of Transport introduces legislation to funnel hundreds of millions of dollars to the railway companies when he does not seem to see the need for such basic things as $500 per car worth of safety modification on hopper cars. Transport Canada's reluctance in this regard makes true sceptics of us when we hear promises to strictly monitor railway performance in return for the windfall of higher freight rates.
[DOT] (M40)
The secretary-treasurer of the grain services union says that something as basic as $500 worth of safety monitoring devices on a hopper car would make things so much better and easier for the workers who handle those hopper cars. It would make things much safer in terms of physical health and mental health by relieving anxiety about the possibility of being injured.
I do not know whether the secretary-treasurer of the grain services union is right or wrong and I do not know whether we are dealing with $500 or $800, but I do know one thing from what he has said and that is that worries, concerns and anxieties exist about the safety of hopper cars. It seems to me that if more workers were on the boards of directors of comapnies, on transportation committees and on advisory councils, these kinds of concerns would be heard by everyone involved and there would be a much greater chance of remedying concerns of this sort which would hopefully create a more efficient system for farmers and everyone else in Canada. That, Mr. Speaker, must be our objective.
As 1 have said before, 1 hope that we can begin to establish that objective and set a precedent for all industries in Canada.
I have seen the operation of many industries in my constituency and I know that in most cases the people who are able to give the best advice about managing the company on a day to day basis are the workers who work for that company. They know the best way to load a car and the best way to organize an assembly line, because that is their livelihood and they do it all the time.
1 think the time has come to start practising economic democracy in the country. We must extend political democracy to include economic democracy so that, regardless of one's income, one has some real clout in a democratic sense over what happens to the economy. I think that is what Motion No. 31, if accepted, will do in a very minor way.
October 3, 1983

1 am pleading, Mr. Speaker, for the country to go in that direction. If we were to go in that direction, 1 think we would have a much better system and a much better country with greater equality and greater freedom for each and every person who lives in the country.
Why are we so cautious and conservative, Mr. Speaker? Why do we not become a bit bolder and give more power to the ordinary people? Why do we not decentralize our institutions and allow for more local control? Time and time again, I hear from the business community, from members of the Conservative Party and members of the Liberal Party that we must give more control to the businessman and to the private sector, that there must be more decentralization, more control of the economy, more incentives and the like. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, what about more control for the ordinary citizens of Canada? What about giving more control to the ordinary workers and the ordinary farmers of the country so that they can participate in the decisions that affect the direction the country is taking? What about decentralizing the power and putting it back in the hands of the ordinary people? I assure you that that would work very well, Mr. Speaker.
In my Province there is a very decentralized agricultural system. We have a country elevator system and the Wheat Pool is dominant. The Wheat Pool is a company that is owned by the farmers themselves and farmers are workers in every sense of the word. They have organized the largest grain handling company in the country and they have done it very efficiently and very well. It has worked well for Canada and it has worked well for the farmers themselves. We can use that as an example to show the many other industries in Canada how ordinary folk, regardless of their income, can make a great many important decisions.
Instead of worshiping the mighty dollar, 1 wish that members of the Conservative Party would begin to worship the ordinary farmer, worker and consumer in the country. If they did that, the whole country would be much better off. Have I run out of time?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes of the time of the House to speak to this amendment. It is interesting that 1 should speak after a Member of the New Democratic Party has spoken. As a former psychologist, I can sometimes see the consistency in the way some people use language and language structure. The concern about power and control that is expressed through the repeated use of those words characterizes, I think, much of what goes wrong in the minds of NDP Members. Their basic philosophy is that they would have Government control an
Western Grain Transportation Act
increasing number of Crown corporations. They are really asking for control to be placed in the hands of fewer people. It is a basic contradiction. The Conservative Party of Canada, Mr. Speaker, with its concern for the diffusion of power into the hands of many, many different people, is striving for the exact opposite of what the NDP strives for.
I stand in the House today to deal with one aspect of the Crow Bill, this specific amendment. It is a very good amendment and, if passed, would see that labour is represented in a way that allows it to co-operate in moving grain. It is a positive development, Mr. Speaker.
There is sometimes a sense of desperation on the part of Opposition Members, both of the New Democratic Party and the Conservative Party, about what the Government is trying to do with the Crow situation. Before Members of the New Democratic Party attempt to run away with the thought that they are strongly opposed to this piece of legislation, 1 think it is wise to remind the House that the only reason we are faced with this piece of legislation is that Members of the New Democratic Party combined with Members of the Liberal Party to get rid of a Government that was moving grain. The New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party threw that Government out of office. We are now faced with this legislation which will not do western Canada and Canada in general a whole lot of good and in fact may do it a whole lot of harm simply because Members of the NDP put the Liberal Party back in office. In their search for power and control over all of the affairs of the nation, it is the Members of the NDP who make us stand today to deal with the Crow Bill.
If Members of the New Democratic Party had been concerned about western Canadian small businessmen, farmers, yound people and Canadian people in general, they would have gone along with the budget which the Canadian Welfare Council called the fairest to poor people in the decade of the seventies. That is the budget that Members of the New Democratic Party stood up and defeated, throwing the country into an election and giving us the Crow Bill.
It is sometimes difficult for me to sit in the House and listen to my own Party's positions being so badly mangled and misinterpreted. The Conservative Party of Canada is the only Party in Canadian federal politics that consistently, in all areas of human endeavour, speaks about the need for co-operation. The alacrity with which we are prepared to support this amendment is simply one small example of the continuing commitment on the part of this Party to co-operative federalism and to co-operation in the affairs of mankind. Yes, Mr. Speaker, this proposed amendment takes us one small, necessary step toward co-operation in the grain handling industry.
We all know that a work stoppage in the grain handling industry is hard on the workers, hard on the companies and is even harder on the farmers and the customers. Every time we come to confrontation, we create victims. Our approach has always been consistent and it is to seek and move toward co-operation on every conceivable occasion. We should cooperate with provincial Governments, with labour, with large business and with small business.

Western Grain Transportation Act Canada is a nation of immense geographic size with a relatively tiny population. Each time that we forget the need to co-operate and replace that need with an attitude of confrontation, we hurt ourselves and we hurt succeeding generations.
Much of the difficulty in this country has come about in the last 15 years because the Liberal Party of Canada, joined by the New Democratic Party, seeks power for themselves, power over the lives of Canadians by some small elite group. That is the philosophical ideology which guides both of those Parties in this House, and it inevitably creates confrontation. When one tries to centralize power in the hands of a few, it will be resisted by free people who want the diffusion and decentralization of that power.
I would be happier, Mr. Speaker, if we had an amendment before us today which would create a full voting member. However, we are prepared to support this amendment because it is a small step in the direction of co-operation. It is a small step in the diffusion of power. I commend the NDP for giving up their usual approach of centralizing power in the hands of the few and presenting this amendment for which I urge the support of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I had not really intended to enter into this debate. However, I feel it is time to clear up the muddy waters. Our Party would have preferred that an amendment be accepted by the Government which would have made the labour representative a full voting member of the board. In fact, we were tempted to move such an amendment in committee. It was ruled out of order because the decision was made that that would require an expenditure by the Government and, quite clearly, the opposition is not in a position to move an amendment which requires an expenditure by the Government. That is the way the rules operate.
We accept, somewhat reluctantly, that the only way we can get those people who are so vitally concerned about the transportation system and whose co-operation is so desperately needed on the board, or at least to be heard by the board on an ongoing basis, is to have them as non-voting members; in other words, to have them as observers.
Our position, in terms of worker participation, is consistent with the positions which have been taken by this Party since its inception. For example, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), who is just about to depart from this House, would have read in his previous incarnation some of the statements of this Party made at its founding convention, and statements of this Party made at subsequent conventions, where we very strongly advocated the participation of larger and larger numbers of people involved in the decisions of government. In fact, we were true to that philosophy in December of 1979 when the Conservative Party, then the government in office, brought forward a budget which we anticipated did not enjoy the widespread support of the people of Canada. We moved a motion condemning that Party for moving to subject the people of this country to usurious taxes.
There was an election held subsequent to our decision to oppose the government and, by golly, we were right. The people of Canada, given the opportunity to vote on the budget of the Conservative Party in 1979, voted it out of office. If that is not an example of our commitment to participatory democracy, what is? How could we have involved more people in that decision than to have given the Canadian public an opportunity to cast its vote? I say to the Hon. Member for Calgary West, we were consistent right down the line, as we always are. It strikes me as odd that the Hon. Member's days of studying philosophy did not allow him to study it in sufficient depth so that he could see the consistency of what this Party has said.
What aggravates me, Mr. Speaker, is that here we are, as usual, fighting on behalf of the people of Canada to give them some way of having their say in the decisions made by government, and we are thwarted at almost every turn by the Tories. The Conservative Party, reluctantly, at the last moment, recognizing that there is some support for what we are proposing, gives its begrudging support to what it is we are trying to do.
1 put to you, Mr. Speaker, that what this Party wants to see in this country is exemplified by what we have proposed in committee by asking that those people who are most actively involved in the transportation system be given a full voting place on the board, and subsequently, because that was not permitted, to give them observer status at least. What we are attempting to provide for those people is what we would like to see provided on all boards of all commissions for all the operations of government. The people of Canada must be given an opportunity to say what they believe is in their best interests.
We want to see those who are most affected, which in this case would be the employees of the transportation company, those people who, frankly, are most eligible, take part in the discussions which would affect their day to day lives. I know that that kind of thinking is foreign to the Conservative Party.
I know it has difficulty coming to grips with that kind of proposal. I am surprised, however, that the Liberal Party is having difficulty coming to grips with it. I can understand that the belief of the Conservative Party has historically been that those with the money should have the say. I can understand that and can well appreciate that the attitude of the Conservative Party has always been that those who own everything should be the ones who have the say and the workers should never be heard from. That Party has been anti-union since its inception. It became a political party in order to oppose the trade union movement. It is just that simple. Margaret Thatcher will never be out of favour in Canada as long as there is a Tory Party here to stand up and spout her garbage. But let me say I am disappointed with the Liberal Party. I would have thought it might have accepted representatives of labour as fully-fledged members of the board in order to have their input, accepting the fact that they also should be part of the board and answerable for its decisions.
October 3, 1983

1 believe this is the appropriate way to make these boards work. Labour does not want to be a sort of adjunct. It is quite prepared to sit down and be part of the discussions, to come to decisions and to stand up and defend those decisions before the public. The only way to guarantee it that opportunity is to include labour among the fully-fledged members.
As 1 think about it, I cannot understand why the Minister himself would not have agreed that observer status in this instance is not enough. It is denying a very significant segment of the industry which is most involved in this particular legislation an opportunity to accept its responsibility and to take part. 1 would urge upon the Minister that he divorce himself from the Conservative philosophy that those with all the power should be given more. I urge him to recognize the need to involve the workers and their representatives. The railroads, in particular, I might say, would work an awful lot better if some attention were paid to the people who do the work out on the lines, the people who have to get the trains from where they are to where they have to be, through all of the difficulties. 1 would urge the Minister, given the fact he has already accepted that labour should be given observer status, to go even further. Even though he would not have the support of the Conservative Party-which, frankly, 1 do not care about-he would certainly have our support.

Mr. Speaker,
I am pleased to participate in the debate on Motion No. 31 to give official observer status to representatives of the workers who perform the important task of cleaning, loading and transporting grain.
1 want to take issue with the fact that this motion gives only observer status to labour. 1 would urge the Government to reconsider that. We are going to see massive improvements to our transportation system which could affect many workers right across Canada.
I want to speak about my riding for a moment, where a large amount of the money will be going in double tracking, retunnelling and a new diesel maintenance shop in Golden. In places like Revelstoke these changes could mean the relocation of many workers from Revelstoke, a divisional point on CP Rail. It would mean the relocation of mechanical workers from a small place called Field, British Columbia. These people are already subject to very tough Government measures regarding living in the parks. If they wish to sell their home, they must sell it to someone who has a need to reside in the park. But if they move to Golden, how will they do that because there will be no railway workers to live within the parks?
These are the kinds of concerns labour has, and they should have some say in what is happening. A long-time divisional point like Revelstoke has a population of about 9,000. If 1,000 of those workers are relocated to a place like Golden, which could happen, I think it is imperative that labour have someone sitting on this Committee to discuss the concerns of that community which would lose a major part of its payroll.
Western Grain Transportation Act Labour should have the right to vote, not merely that of an observer.
We have seen, Mr. Speaker, some of the ramifications of the Conservative type of legislation in British Columbia, legislation which was brought in without proper consultation with labour. It is sad, sad, sad that the Liberal-Conservative Government in British Columbia has moulded itself together virtually to roll back labour's voice in the communication which takes place between Government, labour and the people.
It is imperative, Mr. Speaker, that labour have a voice and full voting privileges. It is imperative that labour have full knowledge of what is taking place so we do not have the confrontation we have had in the past. It is high time that Canada started to recognize we should have full co-operation between labour, management, business and community so that we do not have to face the kind of conflict we see today where Government comes in and arbitrarily rolls back the advances made in human rights and other issues. Labour has to have a voice in negotiations which take place. In Revelstoke the CP payroll alone is about $1.5 million a month. If they were to lose that payroll, can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, what would happen to that community? These are the kinds of things that labour must be able to sit down and discuss to find ways of resolving these issues. If it means a better economic system of transportating the grain, that is well and good. But labour and management must be able to sit down and come up with some kind of program to offset the kind of changes being made.
To use the taxpayers' money, Mr. Speaker, to upgrade a rail system, and at the same time virtually destroy a community and its workers, 1 think is wrong. Labour must be involved, along with the other groups, and they must have the right to full representation and the right to vote.

Motion No. 31 (Mr. Benjamin) agreed to.

Motion No. 32
That Bill C-155 be amended in Clause 13 by striking out lines 10 and II at page 7 and substituting the following therefor:
"an employee of the Canadian Wheat Board'.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to speak on Motion No. 32 which takes the position that the Canadian Wheat Board is the most important of the agencies to take part in the movement of grain. The reason for putting this amendment before the House is that we recognize that marketing and transportation are so closely linked that it is impossible to control one without having some control over the other. By making the administrator an employee of the

October 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
Wheat Board, we would be making sure that linkage was there continuously.
In the presentation of the Canadian Wheat Board to the Committee they indicated some disturbance about what might happen in the development of a committee which had as much power as the Senior Grain Transportation Committee and was not related to marketing as closely as it should be. The Wheat Board is an agency established under legislation passed by this Parliament in 1935. It has three basic responsibilities. One is to market the wheat barley and oats. I will not go into them specifically but I think they have to be put before the House. Second, it had a responsibility to provide price stabilization for the farmers for those grains which it held by annual pooling. Third, it attempts to assure every individual farmer of a portion of the market available in any particular year.
The result of the Wheat Board controlling the marketing of grain has been that whether one lives in Peace River or as close to Thunder Bay as possible, one still has a fair proportion of the market in any particular year, which is quite different from the situation with which I grew up, when the amount of grain that could be sold in northern Saskatchewan was relative, possible only when the grain near to the ports had already been sold.
I would like to place in context the real need for the relationship between marketing and transportation. Mr. Jarvis, who is the Chief Commissioner for the Canadian Wheat Board, stated before the committee:
The Canadian Wheat Board, like any other sales organization, must control shipment of its own products in order to ensure performance. For these reasons, the Board has always held the view that overall control of the system, as it is developed in co-ordination with the total of the grain industry, should be administered by the Board.
In the last number of years since the Conservative Government's short term in office, we have established the Grain Transportation Agency. Although Mr. Jarvis did not suggest that the Agency was entirely useless, he suggested the extension of that kind of power to a group which had more responsibility might effectively eliminate the relationship between the Wheat Board and transportation. Consequently, he went on to state:
The Board still feels that the system operates most efficiently and effectively if grain transportation is fully coordinated by the major sales agency. If this is not permitted, it should be clear that we view any further reduction in the Board's ability to coordinate transportation as a very serious step backward for the export sales program for western Canadian grains.
What Mr. Jarvis was attempting to point out to the committee was that if one separates the responsibility for transportation so far from marketing, one finds no assurance that products which have been sold will get to the consumers, and that instead of improving the transportation system it may become worse than it is at present. It has been doing a pretty good job in the last while, and I think much of that can be attributed to the fact that the Canadian Wheat Board has been the main agency in controlling both sales and transportation. If the two are separated, it is bound to affect the
efficiency and the effectiveness of the total grain sales operation. Mr. Jarvis went on to state:
Our strong concern is that with the establishment or a grain transportation agency by bill C-155 and under Section 97 (b) of the Canada Grain Act, further powers could readily be shifted by order in council from the Canadian Wheat Board to this agency at a later date.
That in itself is a very great danger to every farmer who has derived a great deal of security from the Canadian Wheat Board, which is a Government agency but one operated on behalf of, and financed by, the farmers. 1 want Your Honour to know that no money from the taxpayers of Canada goes into the operation of the Canadian Wheat Board. The sale and marketing of Canadian grains by the Canadian Wheat Board is financed entirely by the farmers. Therefore, since what we are discussing in this Transportation Act is the movement of grain, it is very important that we have the kind of control over that movement which allows the farmers' agency to operate well and effectively. If we do not, we will be doing a real disservice to the farmers.
It is possible, as Mr. Jarvis pointed out, that if we do not have a close relationship between the Wheat Board and the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, we will be doing a disservice to the operation. He went on to say:
These powers could include those the board currently has under Section 2l(k) of the Canadian Wheat Board Act which allows the board to operate the block shipping system. Any such transfer in the future would result, we believe, not only in major problems for the efficiency of the transportation system but also for the effectiveness of our sales efforts.
If we allow this kind of situation by passing the Bill without the amendment we are suggesting, we will be contributing to lack of efficiency rather than increased efficiency.

Mr. Speaker, I am most anxious to hear from the Official Opposition in this debate. After all the great words we heard out in Regina and Saskatoon over the weekend, I would like to know where all this fighting to keep the Crow is coming from with regard to the Official Opposition. It seems to me that the Conservatives should be charged with false pretences as an Official Opposition.
The amendment under discussion is in accordance with the wishes of 90 per cent of the grain producers in western Canada who support orderly marketing and want to see the Wheat Board strengthened, not weakened. This legislation undermines and weakens-in fact, attacks-the Canadian Wheat Board. It will allow for the removal of certain powers. The Bill would set up one man, the Grain Transportation Administrator, as an agency. This agency, of course, even though it is comprised of only one man, has all the powers of any government agency.
We already have at least four agencies involved in the handling and transportation of grain: the Canadian Wheat Board, the Canada Grain Commission, the Canadian Transportation Commission, the Railway Committee and the Marine Committee. This legislation inserts an additional agency into this mix.
October 3, 1983

My colleague, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), quoted the Chief Commissioner for the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. Jarvis. I want to quote the words of a well-known and respected figure in western Canada, one who served about ten or 12 years as President of the Sask Wheat Pool and then another dozen or so years as Commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board. I refer to one Charlie Gibbings, who the committee voted not to invite and then voted to invite. When he could not come on the day they chose, they then voted not to invite him. We will also remember that out West.
Other colleagues will be quoting the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee, the National Farmers Union and other organizations who want the authority envisaged in this legislation left with the Canadian Wheat Board. But let me quote Mr. Gibbings:
As this committee has been told before, it is imperative that grain sales and grain transportation not be separated.
The Wheat Board Advisory Committee has told us repeatedly that the marketing and sale of grain are inextricably linked to the transportation of that product and that transportation is vital to the success of marketing and sale by the Canadian Wheat Board. That is $6 billion worth of export grain in addition to whatever we consume in Canada.
Mr. Gibbings goes on to say:
The Canadian Wheat Board must be able to arrange transportation of its own product, or it cannot fulfil its obligations to Western grain producers or their customers overseas. The Board's marketing success depends on its ability to make day-by-day or even hour-by-hour decisions on grain movement. Its flexibility must not be compromised.
Providing powers to a Grain Transportation Administrator can do nothing else but compromise and threaten the prospect of the Canadian Wheat Board's ability and flexibility in the marketing and sales to be compromised.
At the moment we have a Grain Transportation Co-ordinator who works closely with the Canadian Wheat Board and Canada Grain Commission. The fact that we are moving record volumes proves that it is working.
The Canada Grain Commission allocates 5 per cent of the cars for individual producers and the Canadian Wheat Board allocates the rest for board and non-board grain under a quota system and a block system. It is working fine. Then why do we need another agency imposed on a group of agencies that are already doing a first-class job? That is why we submit that the Senior Grain Transportation Administrator is one person who should be an employee of the Canadian Wheat Board. This employee-an official, officer or even a commissioner of the Wheat Board appointed by the Minister-operates under the purview of the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board as an agency of Her Majesty.
Every attempt has been made since 1935 to get rid of the Canadian Wheat Board legislation. In more recent years, who has mounted the attacks, the undermining and criticisms? The private grain trade. The Winnipeg Commodity Exchange does
Western Grain Transportation Act not like it. The railroads would like to have most of the say in where the rolling stock goes and when, at their convenience.
Mr. Gibbings pointed out:
We have a group of individuals in the GTA and in Transport Canada whose abstract economic principles tell them that the grain industry has gone the wrong way over the past hundred years. They want to see the transportation system in a certain configuration, and they expect farmers, the grain companies, the Wheat Board, and our customers to adjust to accommodate it.
I suggest the reverse approach be taken. Let the transportation system develop to meet the needs of the people who are using it. That is the approach that makes real economic sense, and the Government should allow it to proceed by keeping bureaucracy out of the grain business.
We have always been operating throughout these decades on the basis of what is best for the railroads. They are a utility which everyone must use both directly and indirectly. Surely the railroads and every other transportation system should function to meet the needs of the shippers and receivers, the loaders and unloaders and the handlers of commodities that are to be moved.
Mr. Gibbings is right on. The situation should be the other way around. Our transportation system should be set up to meet the needs of the people who are using it, instead of the people who have to use it adjusting their operations to suit some people in the Department of Transport and the two railroads.
Most fundamentally of all, the attempt to undermine and reduce the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board has always been with us, particularly since the end of the Second World War. There was legitimate cause for the grain co-operatives and the grain producers to band together and build their own country elevator system to enable our three Prairie Pools and the United Grain Growers to handle some 80 per cent of all our grains. The private grain trade does not like that.
In addition, even the Government of the day in 1935 under R. B. Bennett recognized that there had to be a central marketing and sales organization for Canada's export grains. The subsequent Mackenzie King Government, particularly in the first and second year of World War II, really put the Canadian Wheat Board Act into a functioning state and enlarged its powers. Since the war those powers have been broadened to include the setting up of a block system, the administration of a quota system for the amounts of grain that farmers can deliver and the allocation of the cars to move that grain under those quotas in the block system. Surely that is keeping the railways functioning to meet the needs of the people who must use it.

October 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
Mr. Speaker, once again we witness the NDP grasping for straws, trying to sow the seeds of fear and attempting to create a mountain out of a molehill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: All great Tory tricks.

There is another great farmer from Toronto who wants to get into the debate. Certainly his comments would be welcomed, particularly his expertise.
The NDP are trying to create the impression that the Grain Transportation Administrator will undermine the role of the Canadian Wheat Board. I do not believe that that was ever the intent behind the establishment of a Grain Transportation Co-ordinator or Administrator. Historically, over the last four years I do not think there is any evidence that that has in fact happened. Quite the contrary.
If the NDP are concerned about the possibility of the Wheat Board's integrity being undermined, perhaps they would do well to pass their eyes over Motion No. 39. If passed, this motion would ensure that the provisions of this Act respecting the functions and the duties of the Administrator would not restrict the powers of the Canadian Wheat Board under the Canadian Wheat Board Act to make available the quantities and types of grains necessary to achieve sales in its own behalf and in the interests of producers.
Quite frankly, the evidence that we received during the course of the committee hearings made two or three points very fundamentally clear. The Grain Transportation Administrator was serving a very useful function. His role was supported by all parties involved in the handling and moving of grain, and that should be continued. We heard time and time again during the course of the development of the legislation that all parties to the whole grain handling and transportation system supported the concept of the Grain Administrator.
Our Government established the concept of an administrator in 1979. It was felt at that time there was a clear need for it, and the concept was put in place for a trial period. It was not enshrined in legislative form but as a trial mechanism which has worked very well. I do not think, other than a few radicals, like the Chairman of the Advisory Board to the Canadian Wheat Board and a few other NDP socialists who want to see everything concentrated into one empire, that there is any great amount of negative reaction to the concept of the Administrator.
Let us look briefly at the terms of reference given to the Grain Transportation Authority in 1979. First, the objectives were to increase the grain handling and transportation system s capacity to achieve a 20 per cent increase in exports in 1980 and a 50 per cent increase by 1985 to 30 million tonnes. Those objectives have been achieved.
I do not think the Grain Transportation Authority would suggest for one minute that it achieved those targets on its own. It provided the mechanism wherein all parties could come
together and sort out the difficulties and work together in a cohesive manner. I think that is important. We heard from the NDP about the importance of having all parties at the table to ensure that everyone was aware of their responsibilities and that everyone knew what everyone else was doing. That was really the start of it. While the Grain Transportation Authority did not have a whole lot of legislative authority, it did have a lot of persuasive abilities. It was in that connection that it was able to assist in facilitating the movement of grain and overcome certain bottlenecks.
The second objective of the GTA was to ensure that prairie grain moves to domestic consumption and export positions in a prompt, efficient and orderly manner. Third, its objective was to secure the co-operation and participation of the industries concerned in providing the required transportation and handling services and facilities. Fourth, the GTA was to carry out the required planning and implement the changes necessary to make the forwarding system operate more efficiently and effectively, and to increase its capacity to meet i he 1985 target of a 50 per cent increase in exports. Fifth, it was to keep all parties and the public fully informed about the system's operations and shortcomings.
From that day hence there have been regular documents and publications released by the Grain Transportation Authority which make for some very interesting reading. For example, the January, 1983 "Grain Transportation Update" has the headline "New Grain Exports Records". I have its annual report for the 1981-1982 crop year. In April, 1983 the headline is "Another Record Breaking Winter". It talks about the West Coast performance and some of the difficulties. The August, 1983 headline reads "Canada Exports 28.3 million tonnes".
The GTA does not only publish the good news but it publishes some of the critical news and some of the things that have to be done to be sure all parties are fully informed and aware of the difficulties. I think the GTA works very well. If anything, it has enhanced the integrity of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Prior to 1979 the Canadian Wheat Board was continually embroiled in all the difficulties, arguments, charges and countercharges that were levied at the various players within the system. On frequent occasions the Wheat Board was caught in the middle. I think the Grain Transportation Authority has provided that kind of safety valve and it has taken a lot of the heat that would normally accrue to the Canadian Wheat Board.
In specific terms, what were the responsibilities? First, it took responsibility for the primary allocation and use of the car fleet, including the CN and CP grain-dedicated fleet, Government hopper cars, federal and provincial, and Canadian Wheat Board hopper cars. Second, it allocated railway equipment between the Board and non-Board sectors and between the various users of cars for non-Board grains.
It was in that connection that the role of the Administrator or the Co-ordinator was very important. Because the Board was involved in the allocation of cars, 1 am not suggesting this
October 3, 1983

was the truth but there was a perception that they were unfairly allocating a more favourable proportion to those Board grains and non-Board grains. However, that was overcome to a large extent by the bringing together of all the parties, by letting the public know what was going on and by the Administrator acting as a referee.
Third, the responsibility of the GTA was to develop policies and procedures where necessary to ensure proper functioning of the allocation system. Fourth, it was to determine future needs for rail cars and to make recommendations to the Minister of Transport on the required acquisitions for the grain fleet.
That is another area in which it did an excellent job. It has constantly monitored the hopper car and rolling stock fleet requirements, the cars that were going out of service and the need for additional cars coming on.
The GTA has served a very useful role and it will continue to do so. The important element in terms of this institution is that it must be neutral and function in a neutral way. It must not have any vested interest, either in the Board or in the non-Board side of things. It must have the necessary stature to deal with transportation issues on an equal footing with all participants.
I think that contrary to what my friends in the New Democratic Party suggest, there has been support for the concept of the Co-ordinator and it has come from rather interesting places: for example, a joint submission by the Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. Let me finish with this quote from a submission: "Very important institution. The Pools accept the formal establishment of a grain transportation agency administrator with co-ordinating functions and powers." I can quote further comments of the Chief Commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, who said that they worked very closely with the Grain Administrator but they were concerned about any erosion of powers in so far as the Canadian Wheat Board is concerned. That protected feature is enshrined in the legislation. Therefore, we on this side will be voting against the motion of the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to follow the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). He said our Party was once again, to quote him, "grasping for straws and making a mountain out of a molehill". It is interesting that he would say that because up until now he has been following the leadership of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) in all the motions before the House. If he thinks we are always grasping for straws and making mountains out of molehills, why is he following the leadership of the Hon. Member for Regina West? Last week he supported the amendment by the Hon. Member for Regina West to move from one member to three members the Wheat Pool membership on the Senior Grain Advisory Committee. He also supported our amendment to make sure that Wheat Pool committee men, chairmen and secretaries could seek office. Today he is supporting another motion to ensure that labour has a voice on the Committee. He
Western Grain Transportation Act
has taken his Party and the leadership of his Party very, very seriously. He is taking his cue from this side of the House. It is very ironic that he has to say that kind of thing.
He must have some concerns as well because Motion No. 39, in the name of the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), ensures in a legal sense that no power is taken from the Canadian Wheat Board. 1 am sure he must have the concerns we have as well. Once again he is following the leadership of the Hon. Member for Regina West.
Although Motion No. 39 on the Order Paper in a technical and legal sense will make it impossible, if the Government supports it, to take away any of the powers of the Canadian Wheat Board, it is very important that the chief officer or the Administrator of the new Committee be an employee of the Wheat Board. I say that from life's experience. When one looks at organizations, whether it is a political party, a business organization, a volunteer organization or a people's organization, the chief administrating officer has immense discretionary power by virtue of the office; the office is very important. What that person says or does, what staff that person has around him or her, gives that person an awful lot of power. For that reason 1 would like to see the Administrator be an employee of the Wheat Board.
Once again I say that we should listen to the voice of the people. The people in this case are the farmers of the land. They are saying overwhelmingly that Canadian Wheat Board must be the most powerful agency, that the Canadian Wheat Board must be the agency which markets, sells and tries to get them the best price for their grain. Any diluting or weakening is not responding to the wishes of our constituents. I remind my friends in the Conservative Party of that reality. I say this because I believe in democracy and that ordinary citizens have to have more say over the direction of the country.
If we allow the Administrator of this new Committee to be any person whatsoever, with the powers we are giving this person we run the possibility through the discretionary acts of the Administrator of taking away powers from the Canadian Wheat Board. I believe that does not go in the direction the people want, and we in this Chamber are supposed to represent the people.
I am sure as an urban Member, Mr. Speaker, you realize the points I am making are very important. In the Bill the Administrator is given tremendous power. It is said that the Committee may, on its own initiative, or shall, at the request of the Minister or the Administrator, advise and make recommendations to the Minister or the Administrator on any matter affecting transportation, shipping or handling of grain. In other words, immense powers are vested in the Committee and immense powers are vested in the Administrator himself or herself.
The Administrator is appointed for four years. Once the Administrator is appointed, that office, the make-up of the person and the gut feeling of that person about the transportation of grain become extremely important. It is also provided

October 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act in the Bill that the Administrator can be reappointed after his first term in office expires. For reasons like that it is very important that the Administrator be an employee of the Canadian Wheat Board. The Canadian Wheat Board is a farmers' organization. If one were to have a vote in my riding among permit holders, I would venture to say that over 80 per cent or 90 per cent would say that we must strengthen the Wheat Board in every conceivable way. It is as important to the farmers as a trade union is to workers in the Kootenays or as a professional association is to lawyers and doctors of the country. For reasons like that we must ensure that the Administrator is someone who comes from their organization, from the Canadian Wheat Board.
Over many years farmers have fought to build a co-operative movement. They have banded together collectively to help one another, to share and to work for the common good or common cause. They fought for many years. One could speak for hours in the House about the struggle to build the Canadian Wheat Board, about the tremendous problems with the Grain Exchange in Winnipeg, the Richardson family in Winnipeg, the commodities market, the Chicago futures market and the great Depression which was complicated by the fact that there was a drought. People of my grandfather's and father's generation sacrificed much to leave behind an agency or a system which represented the ordinary farmer, which ensured that ordinary farmers, whether small, middle-sized or large, obtained fair prices for their commodities, which ensured quotas, planning and an organization in place that would treat everyone equally. I want to see that organization strengthened. I do not want to see it weakened by default. That possibility is there when we allow the Administrator to have such powers and discretionary bases. Of course, every Administrator will reflect his own ideology and philosophy.
1 say to Hon. Members of all Parties and from all regions that farmers are exemplified or represented by Roy Atkinson, the Chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee. They made very clear in their testimony before the committee that it was very important for the Wheat Board to be supported. It is very important that urban Members from Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal or wherever understand-
Winnipeg-Fort Garry?

I suppose, although he should know, being a westerner. They should understand that the Wheat Board Advisory Committee is elected by farmers. They want to strengthen the Wheat Board and make sure that anything the House does does not deviate from that principle.
I have before me a transcript of the proceedings on August 18. Mr. Roy Atkinson, the Chairman, said-
Another radical socialist.

I hear the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) indicating that he is another radical socialist and that he will not listen to him. I do not know whether or not he respects democracy, whether or not he likes or dislikes Roy Atkinson. This man is the Chairman of the Wheat Board
Advisory Committee in Canada. He probably thinks Peter Lougheed is a socialist. He worships Margaret Thatcher; he is a clone of Margaret Thatcher.
Why didn't you go and hear him if you like him so much?

1 have heard Roy Atkinson many times. He is an old friend. He speaks the will of the people. He speaks for the people. He is the voice of the people. He was elected by grain producers, and that is important. 1 wish the Conservative Party would respect democracy. When we mention the Chairman of the Wheat Board Advisory Committee, they start to laugh and show disrespect for the farmers' own elected person. That is shameful. They rise in the House and talk about the Chamber of Commerce or Iron Ore of Canada, organizations of the elite which represent a small wealthy group, as if they are gods. Then they are snarky and make various kinds of unflattering utterances when we talk about someone who represents the voice of the people, like Roy Atkinson.
I am sure my farmers will be very interested in knowing that the Conservatives do not take the Wheat Board Advisory Committee very seriously at all. When there are elections for that office in my riding, various people participate. For example, in my riding we elected a very brilliant young farmer, Michael Halyk, who sits on the Wheat Board Advisory Committee. He represents us very well. I am sure he would be interested in knowing that the Conservative Party laughs at the Chairman of the Committee and at the work he is doing, just because he happens to be a person who is not afraid to speak out on behalf of Canadian farmers.
Are you starting to rise, Mr. Speaker, or could I have a few mintues to continue? It would be interesting to have some of these quotations on the record, such as the one of Mr. Roy Atkinson.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to speak to Motion No. 32 as it gives us an opportunity to consider a number of matters. It again gives NDP Members an opportunity to say why we oppose this Bill so strenuously, and that is that it threatens the entire way of life on the Prairies. That is not just because of changes to the Crow rate and all that goes along with that. We have gone into the details of this on other occasions. We believe this is part and parcel of a long-term trend which will erode not just the way of life which has been built up on the basis of the statutory grain rate, but the whole economic
October 3, 1983

framework of western Canada, of which the Canadian Wheat Board has been a central part.
It comes as no surprise that Progressive Conservative Members do not support us in this amendment. They are not interested in defending the way of life which has built up over the years in western Canada. That is not clear to many western Canadians yet, but some day it will become clear that that is not on the agenda of the Conservative Party. The Conservatives are not a genuine defender of the way of life that has built up on the Prairies over the years as a result of certain economic institutions like the Canadian Wheat Board and historical arrangements like the Crow rate.
The fact that the Progressive Conservative Party is being picky about this amendment and is not seizing every opportunity, along with us, to reaffirm the role of the Canadian Wheat Board in the Prairie economy is a very clear indication of what we have been saying all along. The Conservatives are in line with the Liberals in so far as the long-term agenda in the West is concerned. What is that? The long-term agenda is fundamentally to transform the economy of western Canada so that western Canadians, in this case grain producers, do not have the control over their own destiny which they formerly had and would like to keep.
It is so that they will have a railway.

They have a railway, can have a railway and will have a railway as long as there is the political will to make the railways do what is necessary in this country. There is absolutely no reason why we should have before us this piece of legislation in order to have a good railway system. My Leader indicated in the House last week that we are prepared to go ahead with a Bill dealing with railway upgrading and expansion. However, we do not believe this should be done on the backs of the Canadian grain producers, unlike the Liberals and Conservatives who have capitulated to the blackmail of the railways in this country.
I come back to the Progressive Conservatives. The people in western Canada know that the Liberals are not their friends, so we do not have to debate that. However, there is still a significant number who believe that, when it comes to this kind of issue, they still have friends in the Progressive Conservative Party. That is not surprising because the Conservatives have taken almost every position they can take on this Bill. They have danced all over the place. They have been on one side of the fence, on the fence, on the other side, back again and then over again. It is very difficult to know what is going on. But, given the historical presence of the Progressive Conservative Party in western Canada, it is not surprising that there are still people who hope that the Party to whom they have given their loyalty over the years is a genuine defender of their interests.
Many western Canadians who do not think so now will come to think in the near future that the Progressive Conservative Party has abandoned the protection of their way of life on the Prairies. That will soon come to be known. They cannot bring themselves to defend this amendment which would reaffirm
Western Grain Transportation Act and reassert the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board because that Board is responsible for orderly marketing.
The Canadian Wheat Board is a symbol in Canada of orderly marketing, the way in which we have tried to protect grain producers and others from the effects of the marketplace. That is something which always rubs Conservatives the wrong way. Yet they have had to accept the Canadian Wheat Board over the years.
I cannot hear what the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) is saying. If he is going to have a bit of a jape between him and his comrades, maybe he could say it a little louder so that I could respond.
It is no surprise that the Progressive Conservative Party is not with us on this amendment, given the constant penetration of the Progressive Conservative Party by neo-conservative American ideas. There has been an abandonment of the Tory tradition in Canada of wanting to build up institutions to protect the common good and the people of Canada. It is not surprising that the Conservatives would not be with us on this amendment to reaffirm and reassert the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board. In their heart of hearts they would like to see orderly marketing in this country eroded. One way they can begin to do that is by allowing step by step the erosion of the Canadian Wheat Board. That will not just have an effect on orderly marketing of grain in this country, but a symbolic effect on the acceptance of orderly marketing throughout the country.
These are the people who normally rant, rave and froth at the mouth about bureaucrats who are not accountable to the elected people, to Parliament or in any other democratic way. Yet they are willing to lay back and take the appointment by Order in Council of one person who will not be accountable to the Canadian Wheat Board, to Parliament, nor be accountable in any of the ways which they always stand up and mouth off about with regard to the kind of accountability they would like to see. When it comes to the crunch, when they have to choose either accountability or their own hidden and not so hidden ideological agenda for orderly marketing in this country, what do we hear? Nothing. We hear the Hon. Member for Vegreville get up and whine about the NDP, as if that was some kind of argument. He has not said why he does not think the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board ought to be asserted in this way in the amendment.
I hope the debate on this amendment will be an opportunity for those who are paying attention to this debate to see clearly once and for all that the Progressive Conservative Party has an agenda other than strengthening the economic institutions that we have built up over the years in western Canada. On this amendment they refuse to come to the defence of the Canadian Wheat Board. With their procrastination on the Crow rate, their indecisiveness and talking out of both sides of their mouths, they have abandoned the whole of western Canada.
May I call it one o'clock?

subtopic: NATIONAL UNIVERSITIES WEEK-FUNDING OF POST-SECONDARY INSTITUTIONS
NATIONAL UNIVERSITIES WEEK-FUNDING OF POST-SECONDARY INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday marked the commencement of Canada's first National Universities Week. Ongoing publicity resulting from the chronic problem of under-funding has often overshadowed the host of positive and important achievements of our colleges and universities. It is hoped, therefore, that National Universities Week will not only underline the problem of under-funding but will also highlight the vital role played by post-secondary institutions.
At the present time, and well into the foreseeable future, universities and colleges are going to be key players in the economic recovery of the country. The technological revolution will require thousands of well trained and highly skilled people, and there will be a premium on those with a high potential for training and those with superior basic skills such as can only be provided by post-secondary schools.
As well, universities have always played an important role in research and development, a function that is becoming increasingly important if not vital to our future. Academics are being called upon to work jointly with business and government toward the application and development of new technology-related products and techniques in Canada.
For some time academics have been warning policy makers that chronic under-funding will result in the inability of institutions to graduate sufficient scientists, researchers, and even teachers, to meet the Government's stated goals. This warning must be heeded.
The motto selected for Canada's first National Universities Week has been well chosen. It is, "We have the future in minds". Might I add that we, the legislators, would do well to mind the future of our colleges and universities.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do not think that is a statement of Government policy. speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question is a very difficult one. It has been addressed in another context by the standing committee with respect to the delivery of foreign aid. I thought the conclusions of the committee were sound because, in the main, the committee did not recommend the suspension or termination of aid in countries where there had been violations of human rights. It did say that where the violations were so gross that aid programs would be inconsequential or inoperative, then that would be a matter to influence not granting, reducing, or terminating aid.
As far as the International Monetary Fund is concerned, to my knowledge there has been no rule, except the general one, that applications should be based and judged upon economic criteria. That has been the Canadian view. Although there have been other countries which have requested that financial issues be judged upon non-financial criteria, we have not endorsed that view up to the present.
