Madam Speaker, I would like to speak this afternoon on Motion No. 32, which is an amendment presented by the New Democratic Party.
What we are trying to establish is the clear authority of the Canadian Wheat Board over the movement of grain. We have no real opposition to the appointment of a Grain Transportation Agency Administrator, as long as that is the person where the buck actually stops. If there is a problem with grain transportation, that individual should be answerable and responsible for co-ordination and efficiency in the movement of grain throughout the country. Very clearly, whoever the Grain Transportation Agency Administrator might be, he must be answerable to the Canadian Wheat Board. The Canadian Wheat Board is recognized, Mr. Speaker, as one of the best, if not the best, orderly market systems, in terms of its sales, its record and its representation of the producers of this country. It may very well be the best agency in the world.
Part of the problem, Mr. Speaker, which I have encountered in grain transportation in my own constituency comes, perhaps, from the lack of boxcars and hopper cars to move the grain out of certain areas. There are a good number of elevators each and every year which are plugged for a good portion of the year, either because there have been no cars into
the siding to haul the grain out, or rail conditions are so bad that cars cannot be loaded up to full capacity. Meadow Lake in my constituency is a good example of an area where the rail is in such poor condition that a hopper car cannot take out a full load of grain because the track cannot physically stand the weight of the loaded hopper car. However, the important problem is when there are no cars at all. I can think of cases where farmers have to haul grain to many small delivery points which are already plugged with grain, and this causes some very real problems. If the elevator is plugged, the local farmer cannot, of course, haul his grain to that elevator. In some cases farmers for many miles around end up hauling grain long distances in order to sell it, especially if they are under the time constraints of a quota. In most cases in which I have made representations to the Canadian Wheat Board, we have been successful in having quotas extended for a period of time. The Canadian Wheat Board understands that sometimes there is a need to extend the quota because the farmers have been unable to deliver by reason of plugged elevators. This is not the fault of the grain company and it is not the fault of the farmer, but it is the fault of the rail companies, I suppose, because the box cars are not there. Or is it the fault of the Grain Transportation Agency? Is it the fault of the CN or the CP or is it the fault of the grain company? It is very difficult to tell. That is why it is important, Mr. Speaker, that the Grain Transportation Agency Administrator who is put in place be responsible solely to the Canadian Wheat Board. The Canadian Wheat Board, of course, is responsible to the members who make up that board, the farmers of Canada.
The fact that the elevators are plugged for a good portion of the year indicates some efficiencies which must exist because there are a number of delivery points within the Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency which do not ship any grain in the wintertime. In fact, there are places like Denholm and Brada and others in various parts of northwestern Saskatchewan which only ship during the busiest times of the year for farmers, which is just before, during and just after harvest, and around seeding time. It seems very unfair to me that there cannot be a consistent flow of grain through the elevators as the farmers hault it in. There are all sorts of reasons why that does not happen right now. That is why I feel that if there is a Grain Transportation Agency Administrator set up, the buck has to stop with that individual. Right now there might be a problem with the grain cars not coming into a certain delivery point. You can call the Grain Transportation Agency and you are told the cars have been allocated. There are so many cars at that siding on Wednesday, for example. Well, on Wednesday the cars do not show up. When a complaint is made, the Grain Transportation Agency says, "The cars were allocated. It is the fault of the rail company. " If a complaint is made to CN or CP, you are told, "Well, we did not have enough cars. We could not deliver them." You are also told that their crews are overworked, that they could not get there, that they have been on a double shift.

We, as Members of Parliament, try to make representations as best we can to the grain companies themselves, because they allocate the cars out to the different blocks. We deal with the transportation agency, which tries to be very helpful. In fact, it goes out of its way to be helpful, but sometimes the situation is beyond its control. We also deal with the Canadian Wheat Board. It is very happy to accommodate and extend the crop year if just cause can be shown. We also have to deal with CN and CP, which seem to be more interested in the main lines and commodities which they can haul to maximize their own profits, especially in terms of Canadian Pacific. It is more interested in upgrading the rail lines in order to haul coal than it is to haul grain because hauling coal is where the real money is.
I suppose that the point we are trying to get across by presenting Motion No. 32 is that there is a need for better co-ordination and better service in the transportation of grain. Mr. Speaker, I would like to echo some of the statements made by my colleague and emphasize a few other reasons as to why we are asking that the Grain Transportation Agency Administrator be made an employee of the Canadian Wheat Board.
The producers know the value of having the Canadian Wheat Board market their grain. In fact, even people writing
Western Grain Transportation Act Canadian history have recognized both the uniqueness and the strength of a marketing agency such as the Canadian Wheat Board. I would like to refer to a comment made by Donald Creighton, a historian, who wrote in Canada's first century. He was talking about the enthusiasm and energy grain growers were putting into a giant new co-operative marketing venture, the Wheat Pool, which only a few years ago they had given to political action. He was referring, of course, to the progressive movement. The Wheat Board had proved to the farmers complete satisfaction that a single selling agency could do more for them than they could do for themselves through ordinary commercial channels.
It is important to recognize the benefits that western Canadian farmers have received from the Canadian Wheat Board. The largest proportion of wheat, oats and barley is produced in the western Provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, with a small proportion being produced in British Columbia as well. The farmers of western Canada are ever mindful of, and grateful for, the fact that the Government of Canada, through an Act of Parliament, has given to the Canadian Wheat Board the sole authority to export wheat, oats or barley grown in their area. Over the years the Canadian Wheat Board has come to handle 90 per cent of the grain exported from Canada.
It is a unique and very important institution to western Canada, Mr. Speaker. By pooling the farmers' grain, the board ensures that the farmer gets a return proportionate to the amount of grain he has delivered. Contrast that with the open market situation which is subject to wide price fluctuations over a short period of time. Farmers did not have access to information which would allow them to make the type of marketing decisions most beneficial to them, but they found that through the Wheat Board they were able to get the best price for the grain. The system had smoothed over the hills and valleys, as it were. That is especially important when you consider some of the northern rural areas of Manitoba.
Because of their presence at committee hearings or because they have availed themselves of the opportunity of looking at briefs, Members will be aware that the Canadian Wheat Board itself indicated its concern regarding the original proposal and the powers of the Administrator as envisioned under the Act without our amendment. The Canadian Wheat Board, like any other sales organization, must control the shipment of its own product in order to ensure performance. For these reasons the board has always held the view that over-all control of the system as developed in co-ordination with the industry should be administered by the board.
Our amendment, Mr. Speaker, seeks to enhance Wheat Board control over the sale and transportation of grain. I might add that the board still feels that the system operates most efficiently and effectively if grain transportation is fully co-ordinated by the major sales agency. It should be clear, Mr. Speaker, that we view any further reduction in the board's ability to co-ordinate transportation as a step backwards for the sales program involving western Canadian grain exports.

Members have previously indicated, the preservation of the Canadian Wheat Board is essential if western agriculture is to remain a healthy and viable industry in western Canada.
The role of the Wheat Board in western Canada is indeed unparalleled anywhere in the world. It is a unique organization, one which should be preserved. We are therefore afraid of what exists in the Act, not so much what is specifically stated but, rather, what is implied, and the powers that it would give the Government to change the Wheat Board in the future by Order in Council. Our concern is that the Wheat Board could be changed by Order in Council at some time in the future and
its authority and powers over transportation eroded. We must only consider the experience of VIA Rail to know that this is not an empty fear but, rather, a real fear.
There have existed, especially with VIA Rail, instances where the Government, through Order in Council, has really taken measures that have reduced the effectiveness of VIA Rail. We are not the only ones who have expressed this fear. I am going to be more specific now. Our strong concern is that with the establishment of a grain transportation agency by Bill C-155 and under Section 97(b) of the Canada Grain Act, further powers could readily be shifted by Order in Council from the Canadian Wheat Board to this agency at a later date. -because we should have realized any new agency would not be content to simply split the car fleet, but rather, would keep looking to expand its own powers.
Therefore, Mr. Jarvis raised two ways in which the powers of the Wheat Board could be eroded. One would be through Orders in Council. Second, the new agency which is being established, would seek, as do many agencies and bureaucracies, to expand its powers and put pressure on the Wheat Board and its ability to fulfil its important role. The Canadian Wheat Board, like any other sales organization, must control shipment of its own product in order to ensure performance. It cannot await the decision of another body. The creation of this agency which Bill C-155 would create, is really only the creation of another layer of bureaucracy. It is just another actor who must be consulted and brought into the picture. It is complicating matters and, in the end, will have a

negative effect on the Canadian Wheat Board being able to perform its duties, duties which it has performed so well in the past.

We maintain that what we have in front of us today, the section that we wish to amend can, and, indeed, most probably will, compromise the ability of the Canadian Wheat Board to fulfil its role.
In Bill C-155 we really find an attack on western agriculture. There are three basic and main pillars in western agriculture. All three of them are attacked, in one way or another, by Bill C-155. The first pillar of western agriculture involves the Wheat Pools, the cooperative effort of the vast majority of farmers in western Canada who pool their efforts together through their organizations, their Wheat Pools. The second major supporting pillar is the Crow rate. The third is the Canadian Wheat Board. All three of them are under some form of attack by Bill C-155. Mr. Gibbings, in his submissions, makes this clear when he said:
We have a group of individuals in the GTA and in Transport Canada whose abstract economic principles tell them that the grain industry has gone the wrong way over the past hundred years. They want to see the transportation system in a certain configuration, and they expect farmers, and the grain companies, the Wheat Board, and the Wheat Board's customers to adjust to accommodate it.
Mr. Gibbings concluded by saying:
I suggest the reverse approach be taken. Let the transportation system develop to meet the needs of the people who are using it. That is the approach that makes real economic sense, and the Government should allow it to proceed by keeping bureaucracy out of the grain business. The Government has repeatedly stated that it will not remove existing responsibilities of the Canadian Wheat Board; yet it proposed to open the door to do so with the expanded Grain Transportation Administrator provided for in Bill C-155. Mr. Gibbings has the same fear that the Wheat Board will be under attack and will have its power eroded over time by what is in Bill C-155. As Mr. Gibbings pointed out in his submission, there are those who consider the development of western agriculture to have gone the wrong way in the last 100 years. They want to reverse it. Who are they? They are the grain companies.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise today to speak to this motion which has the effect of making the Grain Transportation Agency an employee of the Canadian Wheat Board rather than an agency of the Government. I should commence by saying that we are not particularly pleased to have to resort to this type of amendment simply to make the agency an employee of the Canadian Wheat Board. We would prefer that it not be set up as an ongoing entity at all.
In order to make the House understand our position, I would like to point out the background of the present Grain Transportation Agency. Members will recall the years 1976, 1977 and 1978 when we had three bumper crops in a row. Along with those bumper crops there was a combination of labour strife, bad weather, mountain slides and late starts in the shipping season in those ports that freeze up. Above all, there was a tremendous shortage of cars for moving grain.
The railways had not purchased any new grain cars since approximately 1952. Therefore, the fleet of cars was getting old. The existing cars were not maintained, and normal additions were not made to the fleet when those cars were wrecked or removed from service because of their age. The grain companies assumed there was something wrong with the way the Canadian Wheat Board was allocating cars when these problems occurred. No one asked the simple question as to why there were not enough cars being supplied by the railways. The initial pressure was put on the Canadian Wheat Board, whose duty and function it is to arrange for the allocation of cars from the number that are available. Since there was some concern that there was an unfair allocation of cars, the Grain Transportation Authority was established.
That agency used most of the staff from the Wheat Board. It conducted some experiments with allocating cars differently, but I would remind the House that ultimately it reverted to exactly the same method of allocation that was in place before it came into existence. It appears that the agency became useful since figures show that while exports dipped to 18 million tonnes in 1978, it was up to approximately 29 million tonnes by the end of the 1982-83 crop year. However, I think it should be made clear that this increase was not a result of having a Grain Transportation Agency. It was achieved by having people from the Wheat Board continue the allocation system which was used prior to the experiments, which did not prove anything. The old allocation system is still being used. The basic reason for this increase was that there were 8,000 more hopper cars. As a result, more grain could be moved. It was as simple as that.
We have some fears that including the Grain Transportation Agency under this Bill and calling it by a slightly different name will lead to less efficiency. Its chief function seems to be that of taking some of the heat from the grain companies which they used to direct at the Wheat Board. The fact is that the Wheat Board personnel still does most of the work, therefore, it makes eminent sense to keep the Grain Transpor-

October 3, 1983
Adjournment Motion
tation Agency under the Wheat Board, which is an agency which farmers are familiar with and have come to trust.
Our Party as well as the farmers have doubts that a permanent agency will benefit producers. For instance, rather than 18 employees, we understand that the new agency intends to have a working staff of some 35 professionals. We are not sure what they will do, but any new agency whose priority is to double the amount of staff begins to create questions in the minds of people about what sort of power it is attempting to grab and what extra influence it is attempting to impose.
I do not think we should stray from the very straightforward basics of marketing grain. I will point them out because I believe they are fundamental to the kind of car allocation and transportation arrangements that are built into the system. The first priority is to sell the product. Once that potential market is found it must be established which grains and what kind will be purchased in that market. The next step which sometimes causes problems is getting the right grades, the right grains and the right amounts at the right point on the right day. To do that, the marketing agency has to have full control of the process. If it does not, if it is shifted over to another agency as is proposed in this Bill, the chief function and the main reason for that agency to exist is downgraded and undermined. That is why we are afraid of that kind of agency being established on a permanent basis. We think that as a co-operative, short-term entity it functioned and showed that the Wheat Board was fair in its allocation of cars. The facts speak for themselves. The agency ended up adopting the original methodology which the Wheat Board used. This tells me and virtually all observers in western Canada that there was nothing much wrong with the system they had in place. It was eminently fair. It tells me as well that we should look again at setting up an agency that is separate and distinct, otherwise we have one more potential impediment to the completion of that all-important sale of grain from the farm to the final buyer.
We urge Members on both sides of the House to reconsider this agency and to support the amendment which would put it back under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, which has done an excellent job in the past and can continue to do so.

I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker. Everyone we met with encouraged us, under the auspices of the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) who was then Minister of Transport, to establish in a formal way this body called the Senior Grain Transportation Authority and put in place someone who had some authority to allocate between board and non-board grains.
To go back in history, Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member for Lisgar can correct me if I am wrong and elaborate on this, but I recall that when we first started that study in 1979, it was necessary to ship three cars of grain to the west coast to get one car load of the particular grain that was required. That meant that if a carload of No. 1 grain was required, it took three cars to be sure that No. 1 was received because they would end up with a car that contained No. 2, a car that contained No. 3, and a car that contained grain that was lower in protein. These were the concerns that were expressed to us by the system participants whom we consulted with and indeed, Mr. Speaker, by the producers. We felt then, and we still feel, that it is necessary that the Senior Grain Transportation Authority be led by a neutral body and that the co-ordinator or Administrator establish the direction and the fairness that is required so that every producer in the West who tries to deliver grain and has an opportunity to deliver grain has equal access to the system.
Another thing that was done at that time in a very formal way at the cost of Canadian taxpayers was that the railing for the movement of grain passed Thunder Bay. When the Seaway froze, grain moved past Thunder Bay to the Ports of Halifax and Sorel and Saint John. That was done under the auspices of the Administrator of the Senior Grain Transportation Authority or, as that position was then called, the co-ordinator. By doing that, Mr. Speaker, the movement of grain continued throughout the year and did not stop when the Seaway was frozen. Hundreds of thousands of bushels of grain moved by rail from Thunder Bay to ports in the eastern part of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in opposition to the motion before us put forward by Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party. When we look at the question of the growing and selling of grain, the factors of maximizing production and maximizing sales in the international marketplace are all very directly related to the nation's ability to transport and move its grain. What this country needs is an efficient transportation system which will move as large a volume of grain as any of our producers have the capacity to grow. And seeking that objective, it becomes paramount that we have a system of transportation co-ordination which is autonomous with that of marketing. We must have a system which is neutral in relation to that of marketing, because when one takes a look at the whole question of transportation, the enormous complexity of that question must be borne in mind. It is not simply a case of getting a hopper car from some country point to port. There is also the question of the very large number of grades in any one specified grain. The numbers are enormous.
Transportation has to be co-ordinated with the ships coming into port. It has to be co-ordinated with the capacity of the rural points to deliver. I challenge those who believe there is no issue in terms of grain transportatioan to put the simple question to the rural farmers on the Prairies, those permit holders, "Are you satisfied with today's transportation delivery system? I know intuitively that the overwhelming answer will be a rejection of the notion of complete satisfaction, because virtually every community believes there can be an improvement in transportation.
Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party have been arguing essentially with an illogical set of logical-sounding logic. What they are in effect saying is that ducks are good swimmers. "Les is a good swimmer. Les is a duck." Quite frankly, what they are telling us is that the Canadian Wheat Board is good. We in the Conservative Party are saying that some of the authority which the Wheat Board now has ought to go into a special agency, therefore, we are attacking what is
good. The argument simply does not hold, Mr. Speaker. There are many examples of good in which we make divisions. Automobile dealers may have a specialized truck lot apart from their car dealerships. A doctor may practise as an M.D., apart from those who are dentists. If we look at our society we see that in every profession there are examples of good being divided, and a specialization of good would probably equal more good. Hon. Members in the New Democratic Party would have us believe something else. They would like to have us believe that because the Canadian Wheat Board is good- and there is no argument against that-if we did anything at all to remove what is presently within the authority of the Wheat Board to some other agency, that we are attacking what is good. That kind of logic simply means that all NDP Members are ducks and none of them can swim. That simply is not borne on by the facts.
The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Alt-house) earlier this day said that in 1978 the transportation system in this country was a mess. Little did he know that he was making the case for having a specific agency, because it was in 1979, the following year, that such an agency was set up and there was a very significant improvement in grain transportation on the Prairies.
Because we ordered cars three years before that.

I do not know how I would get along, Mr. Speaker, if I did not have the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre helping me. He said it was because they ordered the cars three years before that. That is the point. If in 1979 we had put up the agency and then ordered the cars, it might seem that, well, it is the cars, all confused. But, no, they were there three years before. Yet the Hon. Member said in his speech that in 1978 the system was a mess. Then in 1979, one year after the three years with which he starts, when the agency is in place, he tries to say, "Well, it does not have anything to do with the agency. It was all due to the cars which were ordered three years sooner." That kind of debating, Mr. Speaker, by Hon. Members of the NDP is called "squirrel-cage debating". It means that the faster they run the more they stay the same. There the Hon. Members of the NDP are pedalling away in their squirrel cage, trying to make Canadians believe that somehow the Conservative Party is attacking the Canadian Wheat Board. That is just pure balderdash, and it ought to be recognized as such by Canadian farmers everywhere.
We have indeed 8,500 more hopper cars. We also have an agency which is able to give its full attention to co-ordinating those cars into an active transportation system. Members of the NDP like to speak a lot on this particular Bill. They like to speak when they are recognized. They like to speak when other people are recognized. I would like to challenge them to ask a question in a questionnaire distributed among their farmer permit-holder constituents: "Do you believe, when you have a transportation concern, that you will get more attention by calling the Canadian Wheat Board rather than the transporta-

tion agency?" 1 believe, at least in the area which I represent, there is a belief today that the Canadian Wheat Board is a good agency, but that, in the question of transportation, when it comes to getting action, it is much more effectively done when someone's full concern is focused solely on the question of transportation.
The Hon. Member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewycky) was saying earlier in his speech that the officials of the Canadian Wheat Board have been very helpful. What he was really saying was that since it is helpful, how can we possibly in any way demote the Wheat Board? That was followed on a similar theme by the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) when he said that the Wheat Board is absolutely essential. We find that each of the Hon. Members is implying that because the Wheat Board is good we cannot in any way detract from any of its powers. But what we really need is farmers who can grow to capacity, a Canadian Wheat Board which can market to capacity, and a transportation system which can deliver to capacity.
The autonomy of a transportation system is essential because it is its autonomy which gives it its status. What we want to have is a group of people who are proud to be working for a very efficient transportation system. So when farmers, grain elevators locals or grain elevator companies call the agency, the full focus of attention of that agency should be on transportation. We do not want people who wear a number of hats, one under which they market grain, another for the handling transportation. I believe that kind of separation is important.
I believe the amendment being put forward by the New Democratic Party is not at all in the best interests of the producers of western Canada. In fact, what should happen is that we should achieve a type of system whereby transportation is considerably improved from what it is today. Clearly the farmers at present, Sir, are not happy with their transportation service. They are much happier than they were prior to the establishment of an agency in 1979, but most farmers believe that quotas can become larger and can open more frequently than has traditionally been the practice in this country. In short, I feel it is important to underscore that what we have to maximize is the full capacity of this nation to become a producer, exporter and mover of grain. We must put specialists into all those categories so that not only will the farmers be able to sell all the goods they can grow but we can also deliver them effectively in order to meet and keep our markets.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I add this thought? If producers can deliver their grain much more quickly then they can convert their product into cash, put that cash in the bank and earn interest. They would then be able to avoid a considerable amount of borrowing, on which they have to pay interest, in order to pay their operating expenses. That is all dependent upon transportation. It is a question of how large and how fast quotas open. If the NDP Members do not believe this is very
Western Grain Transportation Act important to the primary producer, then they do not understand farmers and they do them an enormous disservice.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join in this debate very briefly to outline some of the reasons why I personally, along with my Party, would not be able to support the NDP amendment. I would also like to illustrate a number of, for the lack of a better word, red herrings that the NDP Members have dragged into the debate this afternoon, mostly because they are trying to generate scare tactics directed at the majority of grain producers in western Canada.
The first question concerns the Canadian Wheat Board and its acceptability on the Prairies, and whether it is going to be around for a long period of time. In my opinion, and certainly in the opinion of the agricultural producers I represent in southern Manitoba, indeed in all of Manitoba, there is absolutely no question that the Canadian Wheat Board rates as highly now in the esteem of grain producers as it has for a long, long time. Producers in Canada, primarily in the West, feel that while there are some things we could do better with the Wheat Board, the concept, which was put in place many years ago for all the reasons we have heard, is a good one and should remain. No one has said in any way, shape or form that that is going to change. It is not in trouble, although the NDP would like to make it seem that some political Parties would like to decrease, shall we say, the powers of the Wheat Board. That, of course, is utter nonsense.
Some years ago, I, along with two other Members of Parliament, was part of the whole exercise of setting up a grain transportation co-ordinator. It was a great learning experience not only for the committee which I had the honour to chair but also from the point of view of the people with whom we came into contact. The reason the Conservative Party moved to set up that co-ordinator is that we felt, in discussions with the industry, that the direction the industry was taking or wanted to take was unclear. It was unclear to the participants themselves.
It has been mentioned that we held extensive hearings throughout western Canada, into Ontario, parts of Quebec and even in the Maritime Provinces to see just where we should be moving. We found an incredibly complicated system, as I think everyone in this House will realize. We found a system with 160,000 farmers, all individual producers, entrepreneurs or, if you like, small-businessmen. We found a system with two major railways that were in some cases competing against each other, in some cases not possibly as strenuously as they should, but with a large number of employees and a tremendous capital investment in that particular area. We also found many elevator companies which had not only investments on the Prairies, but some substantial investments in facilities in Thunder Bay, the Port of Vancouver and, to a lesser extent, Prince Rupert, as well as investments in the Province of Quebec in elevator facilities.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, all these players, if you like, in this vast complex business of producing and marketing grain have a highly vested interest in the whole system. Rightly so, because they have a lot at stake. Given the number of people

Western Grain Transportation Act involved in this one industry, it was not very surprising that we found friction. We found that unless there was a co-ordinating body to sort out the conflicting interests and in effect set out the direction in which the industry should go based on what the various groups want, over time the industry will virtually pull itself apart. That, in our opinion, was starting to happen when we set out on our task force study.
In our first few meetings it was obvious that the people involved were very cautious about saying too much or doing too much with a group of politicians, which may jeopardize their bargaining position later on. The first meeting we held in which all the participants came together, and that happened to be in Winnipeg, was truly remarkable. While we as a committee had heard from other people that there was dissatisfaction with the system, we did not realize how extensive or deep that dissatisfaction was until we tried to get everyone to sit down and talk out their problems. We could not do it. It was impossible because there was so much distrust within the industry. Over a number of weeks or months, there were a series of meetings. Many times they were with the Canadian Wheat Board, which was distrustful at the start but eventually came around to being of great help. In the final setting up of the grain transportation co-ordinator, the commissioners and the people involved in the Wheat Board were of substantial help. It is true to say that it would not have been set up unless the Wheat Board had given its help and assurance that it was willing to go along with the concept. I believe they saw the need for a co-ordinator because of the distrust that was inherent in the industry at that time. In effect, it made their life a little easier because it took some of the responsibility from them and set it into someone else's area. That of course made it a little easier for them.
So over the period of time we studied this matter, until the transport co-ordinator was appointed, the hostilities and tension surrounding the various participants slowly started to ebb until we could sit down together and have a reasonable discussion and know where we were going. These were all grown men, intelligent people, but they all distrusted each other initially, and obviously they all had a substantial vested interest in an industry which they did not want taken over by anyone else.
What has been the outcome of the appointment of a grain transportation co-ordinator? I think if we look back over the last number of years, one of the things that we can truly be proud of is the establishment of that body. It has helped out substantially. One will find very few people in the grain industry who have very much to say in a negative way about the grain transportation coordinating agency that was set up. The Canadian Wheat Board, the railways, the elevator companies, the three prairie Pools, farmers in general and farmer's organizations all agree that that was certainly one positive step taken under the Clark Government. I think all of us in the House would agree. Therefore, in my opinion, any move which would have a tendency to downgrade that body, even though it would be transferred into another area and made more permanent because of the legislative component attached to it, would be a disservice to the grain industry.
The Canadian Wheat Board, it is true, appeared before the Standing Committee on Transports and indicated some concerns, although in my reading of its brief they were very mild concerns about the direction that the legislative body would take. That is only natural. It was, once again, staking out its position. It was very gently telling the politicians, "Do not go too far because we think we are doing a good job in selling grain. We want to ensure that we maintain that. We want to maintain certain activities that we consider to be important". The politicians have basically said, "Yes, we agree that you will maintain those particular areas, the responsibilities that the Wheat Board has had in the past", and we have proceeded from there.
I have spoken with various officials of the Canadian Wheat Board. My riding is just outside of Winnipeg and, of course, the head office of the Canadian Wheat Board is also in Winnipeg. I can tell Your Honour that its officials are not concerned about the particular aspect of the dilution, shall we say, of their powers.
I return to the point at which I started my remarks by saying that the NDP, for some reason, is using this particular amendment as a simple and pure scare tactic. What Members of the NDP have said here this afternoon in terms of the potential destruction of the Wheat Board, or suggestions that the Conservative Party wants to destroy or in any way downgrade the Wheat Board, amounts to sheer and utter nonsense, and should be taken as such. I cannot support the amendment, and my Party cannot support the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. I know the Hon. Member for Regina West feels that I have done my utmost to be of assistance to him, and that he will see a substantial reduction in my interest in being of assistance to him if he is not prepared to take my rulings on a courteous basis. On debate, Motion No. 32.
October 3, 1983

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak for a few moments this afternoon on Motion No. 32 in the name of my learned friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). I readily admit that I am not a farmer and as such I do not have first hand knowledge of the farming industry. I do represent many farmers and 1 talk to them when I go home to my constituency. I talk to the officials of municipalities, towns and villages in my constituency as well. Over the last few months many of them have passed resolutions which they sent to the federal Government calling upon it to preserve the Crowsnest Pass rates for the transportation of grain. They have done this out of interest for the farmers in their communities and for the economic wellbeing of their communities as service centres to the farming industry.
I have listened today with interest and with some amusement to the speeches in this debate by Members of the Progressive Conservative Party. I especially noted the comments of the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer), who happens to be my neighbour in Manitoba. He charged the New Democratic Party with a poor performance in the debate on the Crowsnest Pass rates or on Bill C-155. This is somewhat amusing. The Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette, in a ringing piece of oratory which will long be remembered, on a day during the debate of Bill C-155 when we had about half the number of Members of the PC Party rising to enter into the debate as Members of this Party-
Come on.
This was from a Party whose Leader on the weekend in Regina and Saskatoon said that it would oppose and do everything it could to stop the Bill.
There were 1,500 Conservatives in Saskatoon; you would have been proud.
Approximately 1,500 Conservatives gave him a subdued applause.
I was there. There was a standing ovation.

Returning to the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette, he spoke about our performance. Today we heard from the hon. psychologist for Calgary who stretched the credibility of the House and insulted the Canadian electorate by intimating that the NDP was responsible for Bill C-155 being introduced in the House of Commons. This is one of the best pieces of creative thinking in the House for some time.
If the Conservative Government had not been chucked out of office in the winter of 1979-80, the Crowsnest Pass freight rates would be long gone, dead and buried. During Question Period today we heard the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) come on as a strong defender of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. He is from the Province of Alberta. I would like to ask him what kind of strong support those rates have from the Premier of that Province or from the provincial Minister of Agriculture. Not very much, I am afraid to say. Who is talking about good performances!
Western Grain Transportation Act
The Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette also talked about this Party's inconsistency in its position on the Crowsnest Pass rates. This Party is the only one that has been consistent from day one. In fact, we have been consistent for many, many years. Our bottom line is that we are opposed to the changes. The Tory position, since the introduction of Bill C-155, has marked one of the most notable turnarounds since St. Paul took a trip toward Damascus.
Once again the Progressive Conservatives are joinging with their ideological bedmates, the Liberals, to put into effect a system which will once again leave western farmers with the short end of the stick. We have them voting against the continued wellbeing o the Canadian Wheat Board and in favour of the ability of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) and the Grain Transportation Administrator to weaken the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board. I say to the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), who is not in the House at the moment, that yes, the Conservatives are voting against good by voting against Motion No. 32.
What are we trying to do with this motion? Basically we are trying to maximize the returns to producers, as was said in the House this afternoon. How do we maximize returns by putting into place two systems which may very well be conflicting, by putting in place two bosses? If you have split responsibility, in the end nobody is responsible. The Canadian Wheat Board has been doing its job well for 40 or 50 years. I do not see why that has to be changed now. If we look at the record of the Grain Transportation Agency since it has been in place, what it has done over the last two or three years is to experiment with systems. In the end, it has gone back to the same Canadian Wheat Board allocation system it was using before. Basically, it has done nothing. It is an extra cog in the wheel, a cog that takes time, could possibly add confusion and in the end would not serve the best interests of western producers.
I listened with interest to the comments of the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta). He said that in his travels in and out of Winnipeg, he often spoke with members of the Canadian Wheat Board who expressed to him that they are not especially concerned with this provision of the Bill. That flies in the face of the testimony which the Canadian Wheat Board gave when it appeared before the Transport Committee over the last couple of months. I quote from their presentation;
The Canadian Wheat Board, like any other sales organization, must control shipment of its own product in order to ensure performance. For these reasons the Board has always held the view that overall control of the system, as developed in co-ordination with the industry, should be administered by the Board.
The Board still feels that the system operates most efficiently and effectively if grain transportation is fully co-ordinated by the major sales agency. If this is not permitted, it should be clear that we view any further reduction in the Board's ability to co-ordinate transportation, as a very serious step backward for the export sales program for western Canadian grains.
That seems to be completely contradictory to the statement of the Hon. Member for Lisgar. We should take note of that. The Canadian Wheat Board has done the job well for many years. It has concerns about the grain transportation authority.

October 3, 1983
27696___________________________________________
Western Grain Transportation Act
We must address those concerns and make the grain transportation authority part and parcel of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Basically, we want an efficient system that will not have conflicts, not have two bosses, two systems working against the best interests of Canadian farmers. I therefore ask all Members, especially the Conservative Party which is trying to pretend it is the defender of the Crow and western farmers, to support Motion No. 32.

Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with interest to the comments of some of my Conservative colleagues. At first I was surprised at the anti-Wheat Board attitude they displayed. I thought as I listened to them, particularly those from the Prairies, that perhaps they were trying to develop some other arguments, sustainable by factual information, which had shown conclusively that this move was going to be of lasting benefit. I then came to the conclusion that I should not have been so surprised, looking back over the history of debate on this legislation; the weak-kneed, lily-livered approach they have taken to supporting the farming community in prairie Canada. Almost on bended knee they hoped the Liberals would push this Bill through as it would save them from having to do so later should they ever become a government.
As I listened to the debate on this clause alone, I began to see what was behind the Tory push. This amendment that we offer is aimed at strengthening the transporting of grain to the export markets. What we are talking about is the responsibility that has been taken on by the Wheat Board to find the markets, to ensure that the demand in world terms can be met, and to ensure that the farmers of Canada have available to them the grain transportation system that they need.
It has the responsibility when selling wheat abroad to make sure that the transportation system in place will be available and ready to carry that wheat to the ports so that it can be shipped on time and the grain farmers of western Canada will be assured that their reputation will not suffer at the hands of some other body. That is really what this is all about. I do not understand the Conservative position. It is mind-boggling.
Which position are you talking about?

My colleague asks, "Which position". I can understand him being puzzled about which position, given the numbers of positions that the Conservative Party has taken since the Bill was introduced. As my old friend and colleague from Sudbury would have said, they have more positions than Masters and Johnston, and let me tell you that their intent is not as good as the intent of Masters and Johnston.
Their leader has been speaking in Saskatchewan, speaking in Manitoba, talking to 1,500 Tory flunkies, getting them off their backsides to cheer for useless rhetoric which does not in any way reflect the true Conservative position. We know the true Conservative position because we have taken a look at it. Others across the country are now beginning to look at it.
What is the Conservative position? The Conservative position today is whatever happens to be the most specious, the one that provides them with the shortest run gain, the argument that they can put forward that will satisfy, notwithstanding whatever argument they may have put forward yesterday. I find it improbable. We have the Tories bemoaning the fact that we are trying to protect the interest of the prairie wheat farmers while they, hand-in-glove with the Liberals as usual, support Liberals at every turn in the committee, speaking together as one and representing the same interests, the corporate interest as usual.
The railroad.

My colleague says, the corporate interests, and adds, sotto voce, the railroad, I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I have a number of other comments I want to make. I will wait until tomorrow to complete my remarks.

subtopic: CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFAIRS-REMOVAL OF UREA FORMALDEHYDE FROM MANITOBA HOMES. (B) MANITOBA GOVERNMENT'S NON-COMPLIANCE WITH REGULATIONS
CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFAIRS-REMOVAL OF UREA FORMALDEHYDE FROM MANITOBA HOMES. (B) MANITOBA GOVERNMENT'S NON-COMPLIANCE WITH REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 27, 1983, I posed a question to the Minister of Consumer and Coprorate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) regarding the removal of urea formaldehyde from Manitoba homes. I asked her to respond and thought that I was to receive a progress report on the problems which have occurred in Manitoba because subcontractors are not being paid and liens are being placed against Manitoba home owners. I was shocked by her response. The answer she gave me was nonsense. It was to the effect that her Department did not have contractors and she could not understand the question.
I went on to ask her why the Manitoba NDP Government is not co-operating with the federal Government by giving progress reports about the operations of the different contractors in Manitoba. She informed me that she had no knowledge of the subject. 1 found that very strange, and I will go into that further in just a moment.
I would like to deal with the history of the problem of urea formaldehyde. Lirst the Government recommended urea formaldehyde foam insulation for homes. The Government is now recommending its removal by Government registered firms which have been proven in Manitoba to be unreliable and inexperienced. A performance bond should be a prerequisite for the hiring of these firms. In Manitoba these firms are
October 3, 1983

hiring subscontractors and not paying them. Subcontractors in turn are placing liens against properties they have worked on.
I would like to point out that there is a time limit with regard to liens. If something is not done about a lien within 40 days, the matter ends up in court. I hope the Minister will take some action so that none of these home owners will end up in court regarding payments to contractors and subcontractors.
Home owners are left with uncompleted work. Wires are left hanging, windows are smashed, woodwork is destroyed, exterior walls are torn down and the home owners do not know when to expect the replacement of those walls.
I appreciated receiving a call this morning from someone in the Minister's office. The caller was seeking information about what was going on in Manitoba. I gave her office the addresses of some of the affected home owners and a little bit of background information so that they will know what to look for when a member of the Minister's staff is sent to Manitoba.
I understand that will be this week.
Home owners will be facing a cold Manitoba winter with no protection against the elements. They face two prospects: They may become ill due to formaldehyde gas poisoning or they may become ill due to exposure to weather. Home owners feel that they are at the mercy of the contractors. The Manitoba NDP Government is not reporting names of delinquent firms to the federal Government and obviously the Manitoba Government is not concerned with the plight of these home owners.
Let me tell you about the plight of just one home owner in Manitoba. He will have snow blowing right through his house because the gables are wide open. He has plywood covering the lower part of his home. He has broken an agreement with the contractor and could have a libel suit on his hands. He has had to retain the services of a lawyer at his own expense and has had to repair damage done by the contractor at his own expense. Apparently Consumer and Corporate Affairs has only one person in Winnipeg assigned to deal with these problems. This one person must deal with problems regarding urea formaldehyde in three western Provinces. With those kinds of problems, Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister should look at expanding her staff.
In Toronto, Canada's biggest class action suit has been launched against the federal Government because of the urea formaldehyde situation. If the Government continues in the same manner, more suits can be expected.
On September 27, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs denied knowing about the problems in Manitoba. However, on September 9, a telex was sent to the Minister by Mr. G. J. Markowski, President of HUFFI in Winnipeg, describing the situation. On September 16, that telex was acknowledged by the Minister who said that the matter was under careful consideration. I find it very strange that she could not give me a progress report instead of telling me that she had no knowledge of the subject when I raised the matter in the House. This would clearly indicate that mail is leaving her office signed by someone else and that she is not aware of it.
Adjournment Debate
Why did the Minister mislead the House? What will she do for these home owners? What action is she going to take against the Manitoba NDP Government for not reporting the names of delinquent firms as requested in order to protect the home owners? I would like to remind the Minister again that there are just a few days left to remove some of these liens before the home owners find themselves facing a court action.
I hope I can receive a more satisfactory answer this evening than the one I received last week.

subtopic: CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFAIRS-REMOVAL OF UREA FORMALDEHYDE FROM MANITOBA HOMES. (B) MANITOBA GOVERNMENT'S NON-COMPLIANCE WITH REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that my reply to the question of the Hon. Member last week could have inadvertantly misled the House. I must in all sincerity say that the question he posed offered me no alternative but to answer as I did. The question he asked, as reported at page 27500 of Hansard for September 27, was:
Has the Minister had any consultations with the Manitoba NDP Government as to why it is not conforming to federal Government regulations? Will she work in conjuntion with the Manitoba Government to have the liens removed immediately, have the foam inslation removed, and have the outside sidings replaced?
I replied, and I quote:
The Province of Manitoba has not informed me of the difficulties and I am glad that the Hon. Member is fulfilling his obligations as a Member of Parliament by bringing the matter to my attention.
No, indeed, I have not received a request from the Manitoba Government. I have had no formal request. Yes, I have had a number of requests from people across the country, including people from Manitoba, which we are investigating. I suggest to the Hon. Member that had he posed his question differently I would have given a very different answer. Now I have an opportunity to answer the Hon. Member more fully, I am very pleased to say to him that I was aware of the specific problem in Manitoba and we had, indeed, responded and we are working on it.
The original question put to me by the Hon. Member had really four separate points: my Department's relationship with UFFI contractors; the specific problem of liens in Winnipeg; the question of houses remaining unfinished, and the Government of Manitoba and performance bonds. I would like to deal with all of these points because when we looked back at the question it occurred to us that there were many questions all within the one.
First of all, I will speak about the licensed contractors. The UFFI Centre does not licence contractors but maintains a register of those who have demonstrated their ability to carry out corrective measures for UFFI.
The Hon. Member mentioned provincial involvement and performance bonds. As I understand it, it is not a provincial requirement in Manitoba that contractors post performance bonds. I am not clear on what the Hon. Member was talking about when he mentioned these bonds and I will be pleased to receive details of any problems he thinks may exist.
There is certainly a problem with one contractor in Winnipeg. The UFFI Centre has a system for identifying contrac-

October 3, 1983
Adjournment Debate
tors who seem to be taking on too many contracts for UFFI work for the number of trained employees they have. I should point out, however, there are very few across the country who have tried to do this, although we have had problems, as I said earlier, right across the country. The particular contractor who caused the problem in Winnipeg was identified by this system. As of August 3 he has not been permitted to take on any new work, although he is required to complete the jobs for which he had already contracted. I would like to assure the Hon. Member of this.
Nevertheless, the situation is not as bleak as my hon. colleague seems to fear. The contractor in question has made arrangements with two of the suppliers who had imposed the liens. I am aware of about 60 liens. I would be interested to have details of the 150 which were mentioned by the Hon. Member. Those suppliers have agreed to continue to supply the contractor as long as the home owners agree to make their payments to the contractor and the supplier jointly. The contractor is confident he will have all his outstanding contracts completed by December 15. UFFI Centre officials will be monitoring his progress.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-DENIAL OF ACCESS TO TRAINING FOR GRADE SIX EDUCATED WORKERS. (B) POLICY INQUIRY
EMPLOYMENT-DENIAL OF ACCESS TO TRAINING FOR GRADE SIX EDUCATED WORKERS. (B) POLICY INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on two separate occasions I have raised a question with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) regarding a policy which presently exists in the Canada Manpower offices across the country, in that it is denying training assistance to adult Canadians who apply for training and who have functional grade seven or less as their level of education. Manpower offices, by policy, denied them admittance or the necessary support for training programs. Twice I have raised this in the House. The last time the Minister followed it up with a letter from which I will quote from as follows:
A careful evaluation of the Canada Manpower Training Program confirmed that academic upgrading at lower levels rarely led to further skill training or to employment. In view of these findings and the Senate Committee recommendations, it was determined that the Commission should withdraw from low-level BTSD funding at the Grades 1 to 7 level.
I find it most objectionable, Mr. Speaker, that in this time of unemployment and misery across the country a Government would set a policy denying admittance to Manpower Training Programs because people do not have an education, the very
people we should be helping. That is a fact; I have it in writing from the Minister.
I also have a letter from Frontier College which came across my desk today, one portion of which I would like to read, as follows:
It is a shock to most Canadians to realize that several million adults have fewer than nine years of school. Of course, for these people, as you suggested, it is extremely difficult to obtain access to provincial or federal training programs.
Mr. Speaker, the Government is denying these people the opportunity to go into training programs, by way of a policy, not by an Act, because an Act like that would not pass this House of Commons. It would discriminate against people because they lack education or because their educational level is not above grade 7. I appeal to the Minister to reconsider this most reprehensible step that the Manpower Offices across the country are taking.
I have a paper from UNESCO which says that 28.4 per cent of Canadian adults have less than grade 9, an educational attainment well below the requirements of our society. The very people we should be helping are being denied that help through a policy implemented by the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
The Government conducted an evaluation which indicated there was no use in giving people who are functionally illiterate an education because they do not go on to take skill training, and do not contribute to society anyway. The Minister also claimed in his letter to me that part of the reason for withdrawing support for those unfortunate people who are functionally illiterate is that the Senate Committee on Finance has determined it is a waste of money. I tell you that it is not a waste of money, Mr. Speaker. If we do not address the problem, if we do not make the people in Canada aware that there are millions of adult Canadians walking the streets of our country who have every right to this education and who, perhaps through an accident of birth, did not get that education when they were young, then they are being denied Manpower Training Programs paid for with tax dollars, programs to which they on many occasions have contributed.
The Frontier College has been teaching people to read and write for years. People coming out of university have gone and worked on train gangs on the railroads to teach people to read and write. This policy is wrong, Mr. Speaker, absolutely wrong and absolutely deplorable. I urge the Minister of Employment and Immigration to reconsider this most reprehensible policy.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-DENIAL OF ACCESS TO TRAINING FOR GRADE SIX EDUCATED WORKERS. (B) POLICY INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for the point he raised, because it is a very essential and important point in dealing with the matter of education in Canada. There is no doubt but that there is too great a number of Canadians, especialy adult Canadians, who do not have the functional education to be part of the labour force in a way that could meet the challenges of industrial conversion with which we are involved at this point in time. However, one thing we must also bear in mind at this same moment is that there are some limitations to

the responsibility of the Government of Canada so far as adult education is concerned, and so far as the primary and secondary levels of education are concerned.
When an adult finds himself or herself in the situation where he or she must go back to school to receive instruction to prepare for training in the new skills that will ensure him or her of the kind of permanent job we are attempting to create in this country, the responsibility, and we must be well aware of this, is essentially, according to our Constitution, the responsibility of the Governments of the Provinces. There is no doubt but that adult education is an essential objective that we must pursue simultaneously with the training of Canadians in those new skills and jobs where the future of the economy of Canada lies.
I am not ready to subscribe to the interpretation that the Hon. Member gave to the Minister's letter to the effect that those people are automatically barred from training. I would rather think that the Minister is certainly not prepared to write off the workers with grade six education. However, the basic responsibility to provide academic upgrading at these low levels rests, in fact, with the Provinces. There is certainly a need on the part of the Provinces to question themselves on their adult education priorities.
There is no doubt that if there are any programs in the country that should address adults personally, they should be for those adults who have reached only the lowest grades of education, because the proof is there on the table that those with very low levels of education have much more difficulty in being successfully trained in order to find permanent jobs. Essentially what we have in mind, therefore, is to establish the minimum skills an adult should have at the beginning, and then integrate the adult in the training programs that the Minister has launched and that the House has approved. Those are the kind of steps that should be taken if we want to achieve the creation of permanent jobs we are all looking for in this country.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-CANADIAN FORCES BASE CHATHAM, N.B. (B) PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT
NATIONAL DEFENCE-CANADIAN FORCES BASE CHATHAM, N.B. (B) PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate having the opportunity of again raising the issue which I raised last week with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais), who now must take the responsibility for the closure of CFB Chatham. Your Honour might recall that last week I asked the Minister how he could reckon his Department's decision
Adjournment Debate
and his endorsement, the decision of his colleague, the former Minister of National Defence, to close the airbase in view of the pledge that was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1976, when he gave his "personal word on CFB Chatham's permanent status". He also went on to say that the base was fulfilling a need and that there were no plans to close it down.
It is interesting that at that particular time, in response to the question, the Minister of National Defence did indeed raise himself to his feet and say that it was the Department's intention to close the base down. I suppose he made the quickest flip-flop the Government has made since it has been in power. Within a matter of seconds he reversed his decision after an interjection by the Hon. Member for Northumber-land-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne). He said it really was not the Government's intention to close the base but just to close down the fighter squadron aspect of it. There is no question that, for all intents and purposes, the base is being closed with the elimination of that fighter squadron. The fact that the F-18s are being transferred to Quebec from Cold Lake, Alberta, means that there will be 3,500 jobs directly or indirectly affected. There will be $33 million in annual revenue lost to that community. It is a community that is already suffering approximately 50 per cent unemployment.
It is also interesting for the House to know that at the last Liberal convention, which was held here in Ottawa, there was a resolution that passed by the full plenary of the Liberal group there gathered which said:
WHEREAS the closure of CFB Chatham would cause irreparable harm to the already struggling economy of the Miramichi, and whereas the recent provincial election has shown the announced closure has greatly diminished the traditional faith of Miramichiers in the Liberal Party-
All of which is extremely true, continues to be true and even more substantial than perhaps it was then. It continued as follows:
Be it resolved that steps be taken that will ensure the current level of employment at CFB Chatham not be reduced.
This motion was passed without dissension by the Liberal Party, which I assume included a clutch of Ministers opposite, and probably the Minister of National Defence, who put their stamp of approval on it.
What has been the response of this Government? It says that in order to compensate for those 3,500 lost jobs it will move the pay directorate of the Armed Forces to the Chatham area. It has promised a trickling of megafunds for some port development and it has maintained that it will establish a fluid bed minerals research centre.
Those projects collectively, with everything else it has announced, will not amount to a 10 per cent replacement of the jobs that will be lost due to the phasing out of the 401 Squadron, which the Minister, and his Department and his Government, are intent on inflicting on those people who are already experiencing 50 per cent unemployment in the area.

October 3, 1983
Adjournment Debate
Today the Deputy Prime Minister rose in his seat in response to a question from my colleague for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and told her, the House and the nation that the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) initiative is a policy of reducing the unemployment rate.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) will apparently respond to my question which more properly should be answered by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais). It is probably an indication of their concern for the area. I want to ask the Government where is that policy for reducing unemployment in the Miramichi region of New Brunswick? Where is it when they stand and say one thing and then create a situation that will eliminate 3,500 jobs instead of creating more. There are no concrete steps whatsoever being undertaken by this Government to begin to address the problems that will result from the loss of those 3,500 jobs, or to reduce substantially the unemployment rate which now exists in the Miramichi area. I ask this Government through this Minister to address that in a positive way; do not give these people words but, rather, bread and butter. Give them jobs.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-CANADIAN FORCES BASE CHATHAM, N.B. (B) PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to update the Hon. Member. I am no longer the Minister of State for Mines, I am the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
I have some difficulty in understanding why the Hon. Member referred back to the situation in 1976 when the Government was just beginning the process of acquiring a new fighter aircraft to replace the CF-101 Voodoo, the CF-104 the Starfighter, and the CF-5.
In his adjournment debate statement on February 9, 1982, and again on April 19, 1983, in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, he seemed to understand the military and strategic reasons the CF-101 operations with the advent of the CF-118 should cease at CFB Chatham, and what the Government was doing to enhance the economic base of the Chatham region.
The then Parliamentary Secretary for National Defence made it very clear, during her response in the adjournment debate, that because of strictly military, strategic considerations and economic needs, it was decided that the CF-18 be based at Cold Lake and Bagotville and that two deployment bases at Comox and Goose Bay would also be used. This decision on the basing posture of the CF-18 had to follow a decision on the best kind of aircraft the Government could afford and what capabilities it possessed. The Hon. Member seemed to understand that very clearly.
In a speech to the Chatham-Newcastle Chamber of Commerce on November 7, 1981, the Minister talked about the standing down of Squadron 416 at CFB Chatham after termination of the CF-101 flying operations on December 31, 1984. The intent of the Government in seeking to establish a broad base for the economic well being of the region was clearly outlined by the then Minister in his statement given in Chatham.
In addition to the current units presently stationed in Chatham, less 416 Squadron, the DND directorate of pay services comprising approximately 350 personnel will be transferred to Chatham starting in 1985 and a building to house this directorate is being built in the downtown core.
An interdepartmental committee on the future of CFB Chatham is continuing its work and proposals encompassing initiatives by the federal, provincial, municipal Governments and private industrial firms, are being considered.
The Minister had constructive and positive discussions with the Mayor of Chatham, the local MLA and the Member from Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) this week. There is an ongoing process of discussion at all levels of Government, and I am optimistic that appropriate activities and initiatives will offset the termination of 101 flying operations.
